Yirui Sun and co-authors challenged a common marker for neural stem cells in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. A surface protein called CD133 is widely used to find and sort stem cells from brain tissue and tumours. Workers had assumed that all such stem cells carry it at all times.

The team showed that human neural stem cells without CD133 can still copy themselves and make all three main brain cell types. Sorting by CD133 alone would miss those cells. The finding urges care in cancer and stem cell work that relies on this one marker.
plos-pone-0005598:
Agi Deguchi and co-authors characterised toxin-making gut bacteria in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Clostridium perfringens type A is found almost everywhere and is a major cause of food-related gut illness. Only strains that make a certain toxin cause most of that illness.

The toxin gene can sit on the chromosome or on a mobile piece of DNA. The team read the genes of type A strains to see how the toxin gene is carried and spread. That helps track outbreaks and judge the risk from strains found in food.
plos-pone-0005698:
Ali Riazi and co-authors traced how a heart gene shapes two other heart factors in 2009. NKX2-5 is a master gene for building the heart, active early in development. It works in a web with other regulators, among them GATA4 and beta-catenin.

Working in heart muscle cells of the ventricle, the team showed NKX2-5 controls the levels of both factors. That control helps set how heart cells grow and take their final form. Faults in NKX2-5 cause heart defects present at birth. Mapping its targets shows where those defects begin and where future fixes might act.
plos-pone-0005798:
Lasse Evensen and co-authors showed in 2009 that vessel support cells supply a growth signal needed to build proper blood vessels. Vessels are more than tubes of endothelium; mural cells wrap them and steady them. During new vessel growth, these support cells are recruited to sprouts.

The team found the signal VEGF must come from the mural cells themselves for organ-like vessel patterns to form. Without that local supply, vessels form badly. The result reframes VEGF, usually cast as an endothelial signal, as a support-cell duty too. It bears on diseases of leaky, chaotic vessels, including tumors.
plos-pone-0006398:
Dormant bacterial spores wake when nutrients signal that growth is possible again. Tetyana Dodatko and colleagues studied germination of Bacillus cereus spores in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Unlike its close relative Bacillus anthracis, B. cereus spores germinate with a single nutrient germinant, inosine.

The spores release alanine, which synergises with inosine to promote germination, per the title. Self-released signals amplify the wake-up call. Understanding germination helps food safety, since waking spores can spoil food. It also matters for decontamination of spore-forming pathogens. Spore wake-up is the first weak point where food safety work can step in.
plos-pone-0006498:
Rahul Sarugaser, Lorraine Hanoun, Armand Keating, and colleagues described how human mesenchymal stem cells organize themselves in PLOS ONE in 2009. These cells, also called mesenchymal progenitor cells, are isolated from many connective tissues. A stem cell is defined by its ability to renew itself and to produce specialized cells. The team asked how that ability is structured in these human cells.

Their title reports that the cells self-renew and differentiate according to a deterministic hierarchy. In other words, the steps follow a set order rather than chance. A predictable hierarchy helps labs grow the right cell types for therapy. It also frames how tissue repair may work.
plos-pone-0006598:
Michael Treadway and co-authors presented a task to measure drive and pleasure loss in PLOS ONE in 2009. Among the traits proposed for major depression, the anhedonic type has strong support. Anhedonia means loss of pleasure and drive. It is thought to show a fault in motivation. The team assessed a lab task called the Effort Expenditure for Rewards Task, or EEfRT for short.

In the task, people choose between easy work for small rewards and hard work for large ones. Their choices give a plain measure of motivation that does not rely on self-report. Such a measure helps test cures aimed at restoring drive. It gives depression research a tool with clear scores.
plos-pone-0009398:
Murni Tio and co-authors published this stem cell study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Mesenchymal stem cells can become many tissues, including nerve-like cells. That range makes them candidates for treating diseases like Parkinson's. Cord blood is one accessible source of these cells.

The team tested three chemical helpers on cord blood derived stem cells. The agents, db-cAMP, IBMX, and retinoic acid, each nudged the cells toward neural fates. They mapped which aspects of nerve differentiation each agent controlled. Knowing the recipe in detail matters if such cells are ever to repair a damaged nervous system.
plos-pone-0009498:
Nicolas Oyane and colleagues used a large health survey in Norway in PLOS ONE in 2010. Many people feel brighter in summer and lower in winter. That trait is called seasonality. The survey, in Hordaland county, asked people about such swings. It also took hard health measures, like blood tests and body measurements, from the same people.

People who reported strong seasonality tended to have worse objective health. The link went beyond mood alone. It showed up across several measured risks. The authors suggest that strong seasonal swings may flag broader health risk. Asking about them could help doctors spot people who need closer checks.
plos-pone-0009598:
Raphael Bourgeas and co-authors built a database for drug design in PLOS ONE in 2010. Many proteins act by touching other proteins. Blocking those touches is a new way to make drugs. Designers need real examples of touch surfaces that known blockers target. The team gathered such cases into the 2P2I database. Each interface was analyzed at the level of atoms.

The database lets researchers compare interfaces that drugs can actually block. That comparison reveals what makes a surface druggable. It gives design teams a reference shelf for a young class of medicines. Such shared resources speed work far beyond a single lab.
plos-pone-0010398:
Octavio Martínez, M. Humberto Reyes-Valdés and Luis Herrera-Estrella argued that cancer makes cells less specialized, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Healthy cells each do a focused job for the body. Tumors lose most of those focused abilities as they grow unchecked. The team measured specialization across the whole set of genes a cell uses. They call that gene set the transcriptome.

In cancer, the transcriptome's specialization dropped compared with normal tissue. Cells seemed to fall back to a general, less distinct program. That view frames cancer as a loss of identity, not just fast growth. It might help explain why tumors behave alike across body parts. A single measure of specialization could also help grade tumors.
plos-pone-0010498:
Yi Zhang, Wendy Schulte, Desmond Pink and colleagues measured how well a shortened diphtheria toxin kills cancer cells in PLOS ONE in 2010. Diphtheria toxin is fearsomely potent; one molecule inside a cell can kill it. Scientists have tried aiming that power at tumors that resist other treatment. A truncated version keeps the killing part while allowing targeting parts to be attached. The team tested cancer cells' sensitivity to the shortened toxin.

Sensitivity varied, and knowing which cells succumb guides design. Targeted toxins promise precision, but only if tumors cannot shrug them off. This study maps part of that landscape. It also weighs safety logic, since normal cells must be spared. Potent natural poisons remain a serious avenue in cancer drug design.
plos-pone-0010598:
Daniel Frank and colleagues surveyed the bacteria living in human noses, in PLOS ONE in 2010. About half of healthy adults carry Staphylococcus aureus in their nostrils. That germ can later cause serious skin, blood, or lung infections in the same person.

The team compared the full mix of nose bacteria in carriers and non-carriers. Carriers held a different balance of species, not just one extra germ. Some neighbors appeared more often alongside Staph, while others were scarce. The pattern suggests the whole nose community helps decide whether Staph can settle in.
plos-pone-0010698:
Chengwei Liang and colleagues searched for tiny gene regulators in a red seaweed, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Porphyra yezoensis is farmed in East Asia and wrapped around sushi as nori. MicroRNAs, short bits of RNA that fine-tune genes, were well known in animals and land plants but barely explored in seaweeds.

Fast sequencing of small RNAs turned up a set of candidate microRNAs in the alga. Computer checks matched them to likely target genes. Finding these regulators in a red alga pushes their known history deeper into the tree of life. The list also gives seaweed breeders new traits to watch.
plos-pone-0010798:
Martin Olofsson and colleagues tested butterfly wing eyespots under dim light, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Many butterflies carry round eyespots near the wing edge. The classic claim is that birds strike the spots instead of the body, and the butterfly escapes with a torn wing. That claim was hard to prove, especially under the low light where many attacks happen.

In trials with birds, marginal eyespots did draw strikes away from the body. The effect held in dim light rich in ultraviolet, matching dawn and dusk conditions. Deflection works when it is needed most. The study turns a textbook story into tested fact, with the light conditions finally right.
plos-pone-0010898:
Koty Sharp, Kim Ritchie, Peter Schupp and co-authors published this coral study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Adult corals teem with microbes, but when those partnerships begin was unknown. Many reef corals reproduce by broadcast spawning, releasing eggs and sperm into the sea, so the team checked whether bacteria are already present at that earliest stage.

They examined eggs, sperm bundles, swimming larvae, and young settled corals from seven spawning species, including staghorn and boulder corals. Bacteria appeared at defined points in early development rather than being simply inherited in the egg. Sharp and colleagues show that coral-microbe partnerships are assembled early in life, not just picked up by adults. Knowing when microbes arrive helps explain how reef corals stay healthy and how disease may take hold.
plos-pone-0010998:
Akihiro Yamashita, Sandi Nishikawa and Derrick Rancourt published this stem cell study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Cartilage formation, chondrogenesis, is a choreographed process that later scaffolds bone, and embryonic stem cells grown in a dish replay much of that choreography. The authors used that replay to break the process into its component stages.

Stem cells differentiating toward cartilage in floating aggregates passed through five overlapping stages. First the cells condensed into clusters, then they became cartilage cells and wove a fiber scaffold, then they laid down the cartilage matrix itself, with later stages maturing the tissue. Yamashita and colleagues turn a continuous-looking transformation into a named sequence of events. A stage map helps tissue engineers check whether lab-grown cartilage is developing on schedule, a need for future joint repair material.
plos-pone-0011098:
Leung, Du, Huang and colleagues published artery research in PLOS ONE in 2010. They studied small gut arteries in rats and a chemical that makes them tighten. Ion channels, tiny gates in cell walls, were suspected to help drive that tightening.

The team found that one class of these gates did contribute to the tightening response. That detail fills in how small arteries control blood flow and pressure. Small arteries matter greatly for overall blood pressure in the body. Work of this kind can point to new targets for drugs against high blood pressure.
plos-pone-0011198:
Jinawath, Vasoontara, Jinawath and colleagues profiled drug resistant ovarian tumors in PLOS ONE in 2010. Some tumors stop responding to a standard platinum drug. Comparing proteins in resistant and sensitive cancers, the team looked for a shared pattern that marks resistance.

Two signaling proteins were jointly raised in the resistant tumors. That pair forms a molecular fingerprint that could flag tumors needing different drugs. It also suggests blocking those signals might restore drug response. For patients whose first treatment fails, such clues guide the choice of second line therapy for each patient.
plos-pone-0011298:
Bousbia, Papazian, La Scola and colleagues reported a surprise lung finding in PLOS ONE in 2010. Patients on ventilators who developed pneumonia had their lung fluid tested for DNA. Alongside germ material, the team detected DNA from plants in the washings of these critically ill patients.

Plant DNA in lungs is unexpected and demands explanation, from food, air or medical materials. The report does not claim plants cause the pneumonia. It does make critical care teams rethink what enters the lungs of ventilated patients. Hygiene and feeding routes may deserve fresh scrutiny in intensive care units.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1298:
The Combined Chiefs of Staff wrote jointly to the State Department and the British Foreign Office on 18 July 1945. The combined body spoke for both Western high commands at once. Addressing both foreign ministries in one letter matched that joint voice.

A letter of this kind carried the soldiers' shared view to the envoys of both nations. It bound the military and foreign arms of the alliance in a single text. This one dates from the summit's second day. It shows the joint staff speaking over the heads of the talks, straight to the two offices that would live with the peace.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1398:
A second Caffery letter to Foreign Minister Bidault dated 1 August 1945 follows in the volume. The text comes from the second Potsdam volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official history series.

Paired letters on one day often split a subject in two: one for the record, one for the harder point. Whatever the split here, the pace tells its own story. Paris and Washington were settling France's role in the postwar order at speed, while the ink dried at Potsdam. Readers following the Caffery and Bidault run get diplomacy at working level, where alliances are kept alive by prompt, exact paper rather than by speeches.
frus-1945-50-intel-d98:
Lyon, acting director of the State Department's Office of Controls, wrote to McCormack on 15 November 1945. The Office of Controls handled sensitive department business such as passports and visas. Foreign Relations of the United States prints it in the later volume covering American intelligence between 1945 and 1950.

An approach from the controls office to the intelligence chief shows the seams where secret work touched the department's public duties. Names, travel, and papers crossed both desks, and the two offices had to agree on how to handle them. Readers gain a finer-grained picture of the State Department here than the top-level fight provides. The intelligence system was not only chiefs and plans; it was also clerks' questions about files, answered in memos like this one.
frus-1945-50-intel-d198:
Minutes record the Fourth Meeting of the National Intelligence Authority on 17 July 1946. It stands as document 198 in the intelligence volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, covering 1945 to 1950. Central intelligence then sat with the National Intelligence Authority, a board of top officials served by the Central Intelligence Group.

Minutes are the formal record of a meeting: who sat in, what was put on the table, and what the group agreed to do. Read with the papers before and after it, the record shows a policy taking shape one meeting at a time. Its worth lies in the trail it leaves: a dated, signed step in the long build-up of the CIA and the Council.
frus-1945-50-intel-d298: Dated 6 August 1948, "Memorandum of Conversation and Understanding" comes from the top level of the government. Readers meet it as document 298 of the Foreign Relations series volume on intelligence from 1945 to 1950. The Council had sent in an outside team to grade the CIA, and the whole town knew a blunt report was coming. A memorandum of conversation is the note a participant or aide wrote after a talk, setting down who was there and what was said.
frus-1945-50-intel-d398:
Fisher Howe, deputy to the State Department's intelligence chief, sent a memo to his boss, W. Park Armstrong, on 8 September 1949. The paper is document 398 in the Foreign Relations volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

Howe and Armstrong led the Bureau of Intelligence and Research, the State Department's team of analysts. A deputy writing to his own chief is staff work at its most basic. Yet such notes set the line the bureau took when it faced the CIA and the military services across the table. The bureau's small staff punched far above its weight through notes of exactly this kind.
frus-1861-d98:
On 14 October 1861, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote a second letter to Lord Lyons. It is document 98 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

The paired letters of that day sort the Anglo American agenda into clean parts. Seward dealt with each point on its own paper, as was his habit. Together the two notes show a full day of work on the tie that mattered most to the Union. The two notes frame a single day of Anglo American business in full. A full day of such business shows how much of the war was fought in ink.
frus-1861-d198:
On 8 July 1861, William H. Seward wrote to Cassius Clay at the Russian court. The letter is document 198 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Seward's July letter to St. Petersburg kept Clay inside the common plan. Even a friendly court had to hear the Union's terms in full. The note shows no post exempt from the Secretary's steady, central hand. No post exempt was Seward's rule, and the Russian file proves it page by page. Page by page proof of the rule is the quiet strength of this whole volume. No post stood outside the common plan.
frus-1861-d298:
Seward wrote again on 12 November 1861, this time to Mr. Robinson. It was printed as Document 298 in the foreign affairs papers sent to the two houses of Congress. It was written in the autumn of the war's first year, while the North worked to block foreign aid to the South.

Readers see the home office side of the exchange, where policy was set before talks began. Letters of this kind are the raw record from which the story of wartime diplomacy is built. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1862-d98:
Writing on 11 July 1862, Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London sent his report to Secretary of State William H. Seward. It was printed as Document 98 in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs for 1862. The date falls in the summer of 1862, the war's second year, when the Union fought to keep foreign powers from backing the South.

Such reports fed the facts and rumors together into one desk in Washington, week by week. Its worth grows in context, as one link in a chain of letters that kept the peace with Europe. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1862-d198:
Document 198 is a note from Lord Lyons, the British minister in Washington, to Secretary of State William H. Seward, dated 4 January in the record of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. It sits among the first papers of the new year in the British file.

Days earlier, Washington had agreed to give up the Confederate envoys taken from the Trent, and the crisis was cooling fast. Lyons stayed in close written touch with Seward as relations steadied. Notes from this turn of the year mark the point where the two governments stepped back from the edge of war. Cases under such notes were often small: one ship, one prisoner, one point of form.
frus-1862-d298:
William L. Dayton reported from Paris on 2 August 1862 in a letter printed as Document 298 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. It went to Secretary of State William H. Seward, opening the August run of the French file.

August began with the Confederate raider Alabama newly escaped from Britain and French troops rebuilding strength in Mexico. Dayton's post touched both stories, since Paris coordinated loosely with London and owned the Mexican venture. His report that week fed Washington's picture of a Europe growing bolder as the Union's summer went badly. French mills wanted Southern cotton, and French yards watched the Union blockade with care.
frus-1862-d398:
On 14 January 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward sent this instruction to Horace J. Perry, the secretary of the American legation in Madrid. It opens the Spanish file as Document 398 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, printed with the President's annual message.

Spain held Cuba, close to the rebellious South, and had just sent troops to Mexico with Britain and France. Washington watched Madrid with care all through the war. Early orders like this one set the tone Perry was to keep at the Spanish court. He was to be firm on Union rights and calm in manner. He was also to watch for any sign that Spain might aid the Confederacy.
frus-1862-d498:
James Shepherd Pike closed April 1862 with a report from The Hague to Secretary of State William H. Seward, dated 30 April. It is Document 498 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, laid before Congress.

Pike's end-of-April letter caught the Dutch reaction to the war's improving Union news, including the fall of New Orleans. The Netherlands, with colonies in the West Indies, had to apply its neutrality rules to real ships in real ports. His reports touched those cases as they arose. For Seward, the Hague file was a steady source of European weather reports. For the reader, Pike's letters stand out in the volume for their plain speech and newsman's eye.
frus-1862-d598:
On 15 December 1861 Spain's minister of state addressed this instruction to General Prim, commander of the Spanish expeditionary force then sailing for Mexico. It is Document 598 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs.

Prim was Spain's plenipotentiary as well as its general, charged with acting alongside Britain and France under their joint convention. Madrid's orders to him, printed here in translation, show what Spain said it wanted in Mexico: debts paid and order restored, not conquest. Read beside Corwin's reports from Mexico City, the letter lets the reader test Spanish words against Spanish conduct. The test runs through the months that followed. In them, Prim judged the French design and withdrew.
frus-1862-d698: On 5 September 1862, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to a Mr. Yrisarri. The letter is document 698 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1862, answering Yrisarri's dispatch of late August. The evidence gives the two names and the date. It does not name Yrisarri's post or land, and the subject of the exchange is not stated.
frus-1863p1-d98:
On 2 March 1863, William H. Seward sent this letter to Charles Francis Adams, the second of twelve he sent him that day in this file. Adams was the American minister in London. The letter is document 98 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

Batch days like 2 March let Washington speak on many heads at once. Each head sat in its own sheet, so Adams could act on them one by one. The London brief held much to sort: claims, ships, talks, and tone. This letter holds one slice of that day's work. Its sense comes from the set it sits in, a full brief laid out in a row.
frus-1863p1-d198:
One of the Secretary's regular instructions to London, this letter from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, is dated 9 May 1863. It appears as document 198 of the 1863 papers. The text is preserved in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume, which gathered the year's diplomatic mail for Congress and the public.

For readers today, these instructions reveal the thinking inside the State Department as clearly as any memoir. They show choices being made in real time, with poor information and high stakes. Alone it settles little; in the run of the volume it helps explain why Britain stayed out of the American war.
frus-1863p1-d298:
On 22 September 1863, orders left Washington for London: Secretary of State William H. Seward to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. The paper is document 298 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. The document comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States, the government's own published record of Civil War diplomacy.

The CSS Alabama, built near Liverpool, had slipped away in 1862 and was raiding Union trade. Washington pressed London to stop such ships and answer for the losses. It belongs to the tense autumn when the fate of two Confederate ironclad rams in British yards hung in the balance. Historians still mine this correspondence for the inside story of Anglo-American relations during the war.
frus-1863p1-d398:
One of Lord Lyons's regular notes to the State Department, this paper to Secretary of State William H. Seward is dated 19 February 1863. It appears as document 398 of the 1863 diplomatic papers. The letter is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, the official series that publishes American diplomatic papers.

Once emancipation became Union policy in January 1863, British protests grew harder to frame. Lyons had to press neutral rights for a government whose public mostly hated slavery. Alone it settles little; in the run of the volume it helps explain why Britain stayed out of the American war.
frus-1863p1-d498:
8 May 1863 is the date on a letter from William H. Seward, Secretary of State to Lord Lyons, the British minister in Washington. At the time, the Union government was fighting the Confederacy at home and working to keep foreign powers neutral. The printed volume gathers the year's diplomatic mail so Congress and the public could see it.

Much of the mail between the two offices turned on ships: the Union blockade, seized cargoes, and Confederate agents buying vessels in British ports. What the page shows is process, not drama. Claims, protests, and replies moved back and forth until small disputes stayed small. That is the use of such a page: not a famous text, but a firm rung in the ladder of the record.
frus-1863p1-d598:
A 1 August 1863 dispatch from Britain's minister in Washington, Lord Lyons reached Secretary of State William H. Seward. The letter is one piece of the steady stream of notes that passed between the two governments in the late summer of 1863. At the time, the Union government was fighting the Confederacy at home and working to keep foreign powers neutral.

For historians, the value lies in the run of the letters. Together they trace, almost day by day, how the Union kept its most dangerous foreign problem from boiling over. Much of the mail between the two offices turned on ships: the Union blockade, seized cargoes, and Confederate agents buying vessels in British ports. Kept with the rest of the 1863 papers, it helps the full story of wartime diplomacy stay traceable, letter by letter.
plos-pbio-0020098:
György Hutvágner, Martin J. Simard, Craig C. Mello, and their group tested a way to block small RNAs in PLOS Biology in 2004. Small RNAs can silence specific genes, a process called RNA interference. The team used short custom molecules that pair with a chosen small RNA and stop it from working.

A clean off switch lets scientists ask what one small RNA does in a living animal. Without it, they can only add silencing, not remove a natural one. The method targets single RNA sequences with care, so side effects stay low. Tools like this helped turn small RNAs from a curiosity into a standard way to probe gene function across biology.
plos-pbio-0020198:
Kyra Oswald-Richter, Stacy M. Grill, Nikki Shariat, and their team examined regulatory T cells and HIV in PLOS Biology in 2004. Regulatory T cells calm the immune system. HIV can infect them, and can also infect normal T cells that have been reprogrammed to act like regulatory ones.

That dual route matters because regulatory cells sit at a control point of immunity. If HIV hides in them or copies their calming tricks, it may quiet the very response meant to fight it. The study maps both natural and reprogrammed cells as targets. Understanding this niche could help explain why HIV persists despite strong immune attacks, and where new therapies might aim.
plos-pbio-0020398:
Audrey P. Gasch, Alan M. Moses, Derek Y. Chiang, and their team compared gene control systems in fungi in PLOS Biology in 2004. Fungi in the ascomycete group include yeast and molds. Their genes are switched by binding sites near each gene, and those sites change as species evolve.

The team tracked how whole control systems were kept, rewired, or lost across these fungi. Some core systems stayed stable for hundreds of millions of years, while others turned over fast. That contrast shows evolution tinkers with control even when the genes themselves stay much the same. The work is a model for studying regulatory change, the part of evolution many now think drives most new traits.
plos-pone-0000098:
Claudia Arce, Carlos Pérez-Plasencia, Aurora González-Fierro, and their team ran an early clinical test in breast cancer in PLOS ONE in 2006. Epigenetic therapy uses drugs that switch silenced genes back on. The team added such therapy to standard chemotherapy given before surgery for locally advanced tumors.

A proof-of-principle study checks whether an idea works at all in patients, before large trials. The authors report the combined treatment could be given and showed signs of activity against the tumors. That green light is the true product of a small study like this. It justifies the cost and effort of proper trials to learn whether the benefit is real.
plos-pone-0000198:
Graham R. Martin, Kerry-Jayne Wilson, J. Martin Wild, and colleagues published this bird senses paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Kiwi are flightless, nocturnal birds from New Zealand that hunt by smell and touch. The authors report that kiwi forego vision in guiding their night activities, relying on their other senses instead.

Most birds are visual animals, so a bird that largely gives up sight is striking. The paper examines the kiwi's eyes and behavior to support that claim. It reframes the kiwi as a mammal-like bird, feeling its way through the dark forest floor. It also informs how this threatened species should be studied and protected.
plos-pone-0000298:
Tamara Glaser, Steven M. Pollard, Austin Smith, and colleagues published this stem cell paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Neural stem cells, called NS cells here, can be grown stuck to a dish and expanded over time. The authors demonstrate their tripotential differentiation: one cell line can produce all three main neural cell types, neurons, astrocytes, and oligodendrocytes.

A stem cell line is only useful if it keeps its full potential while expanding. Showing adherently grown NS cells stay tripotent validates them as a research tool. Such lines support work on brain development and on diseases where specific neural cells are lost.
plos-pone-0000398:
Inês Ribeiro and colleagues studied two genes that pace cell growth in the developing heart, reporting in PLOS ONE in 2007. The genes, Tbx2 and Tbx3, belong to a family of developmental control genes. The team examined how they regulate the dynamics of cell proliferation, the rate at which heart cells multiply, during heart remodeling.

A growing heart must add cells fast enough to build the organ but stop in the right places to shape its chambers. Genes that set the pace of division help draw those boundaries. Understanding their control of heart growth bears on congenital heart defects, which often trace back to errors in these early patterning steps.
plos-pone-0000498:
Joy G. Ghosh, Scott A. Houck, and John I. Clark mapped the working surfaces of a lens chaperone protein, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Human αB crystallin is a molecular chaperone, a helper that keeps other proteins from clumping; in the eye lens it also provides structure. The team identified interactive domains in it that modulate microtubule assembly and disassembly.

Microtubules are the cell's rails and scaffolding, constantly built and taken apart. A chaperone that tunes that cycle connects protein quality control to cell architecture. αB crystallin also appears in brain and muscle. Its mutations cause cataract and muscle disease. So mapping its active regions has reach beyond the eye.
plos-pone-0000598:
Anouk C. Vedder and colleagues compared two replacement enzymes for a rare storage disease, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Fabry disease results from a missing enzyme that leaves fats to accumulate in organs. The comparative trial tested treatment with agalsidase alfa or beta at a dose of 0.2 mg/kg.

Two marketed versions of a therapy invite an obvious question: do they perform alike at the same dose? Head-to-head trials in rare diseases are hard to run because patients are few, making each one valuable. The outcome informs prescribing for a lifelong, expensive treatment.
plos-pone-0000698:
Magalie Lenoir, Fuschia Serre, Lauriane Cantin and colleagues compared the pull of sweetness with the pull of cocaine, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Refined sugars such as sucrose and fructose were absent from most diets until very recently in human history. Today, overconsumption of sugar-rich food helps drive the obesity epidemic. The team asked how strong sugar's reward really is.

Their title states the headline result: intense sweetness surpasses cocaine reward. In plain terms, the sweet option won over the drug option in their tests. A result like that reframes sugar from a soft pleasure to a powerful reward signal. It feeds debate about food design, addiction, and public health.
plos-pone-0000798:
Gerhard Kelter, Daniel Steinbach, Venkata Badireenath Konkimalla and colleagues asked why some tumor cells resist a malaria drug turned cancer drug. Artesunate exerts profound anti-cancer activity, and ferrous iron enhances tumor cells' susceptibility to it. The transferrin receptor, which imports iron by internalizing the carrier protein transferrin, is over-expressed in rapidly growing cells, including many tumors.

Their 2007 PLOS ONE study examines the transferrin receptor and two ABC transporters, ABCB6 and ABCB7, in resistance and differentiation of tumor cells toward artesunate. Transporters can pump drugs out or handle the iron that activates them. Knowing which proteins set sensitivity helps predict which tumors artesunate can treat.
plos-pone-0000898:
Hendrik de Jonge, Rudolf Fehrmann, Eveline de Bont and colleagues set out to choose housekeeping genes on evidence, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Gene studies need steady reference genes to make fair comparisons. The catch is that popular choices such as ACTB and GAPDH can swing widely between samples and conditions.

Unsteady references quietly corrupt results across whole fields. The team weighed candidates against data rather than habit, aiming for references that stay level. Their selection gives labs a safer base for measuring gene activity. The paper is a methods warning as much as a result: check your ruler before you measure.
plos-pone-0000998:
Alexander Sponner, Wolfram Vater, Shamci Monajembashi and colleagues unraveled the layered makeup of spider silk, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Silks are fairly well understood molecule by molecule. How those molecules are organized in layers inside a spun fiber, and what else the fiber contains, was much less clear.

The team linked defined structural elements in dragline silk from the spider Nephila clavipes to their molecular parts. Dragline silk is the famously strong thread spiders use as a lifeline. Mapping its hierarchy helps explain how soft proteins make a fiber tougher than steel by weight. That map also guides attempts to spin artificial silk.
plos-pone-0001098:
Keyue Ding, Samantha McDonough and Iftikhar Kullo found signs of positive selection in part of a cholesterol gene, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Cholesterol balance is kept by tuned control of absorption, liver production and blood clearance. PCSK9, a secreted enzyme, is one of the controllers, and its variants move cholesterol levels strongly.

The team analyzed PCSK9 across fourteen primate species. Positive selection, change favored rather than merely tolerated, showed in the gene's C-terminal domain. Selection on a cholesterol controller hints at dietary pressures in primate history. It also flags which part of the protein evolution could not leave alone.
plos-pone-0001198:
Molecular chaperones help fold proteins inside cells, but they also circulate in the blood and can signal to immune cells. Alireza Shamaei-Tousi and colleagues measured these proteins in patients treated for periodontal disease, gum disease, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Evidence was emerging that chaperones exist in the circulation and can modulate white blood cell function.

The authors report differential regulation of circulating chaperone levels during treatment for periodontal disease. Gum disease is a chronic infection and inflammation, so it offers a window on how local disease affects body-wide signals. Their results connect oral health to the wider immune state.
plos-pone-0001298:
Between 2005 and 2050, the world's population is forecast to grow by 2.7 billion, mostly in low-income countries. Andrew Tatem and colleagues built high-resolution population maps for East Africa to help planners cope, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Census data alone are too coarse: they give totals for districts, not where people actually live.

The authors combined land cover data with census counts to distribute people across the landscape at fine resolution. Growth on that scale has social, economic, and environmental impacts. Maps like these guide where schools, clinics, vaccination campaigns, and aid should go.
plos-pone-0001398:
Daniel Rubio and co-authors wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on stem cells that changed on their own in the lab. The team had earlier found that human stem cells from fat and marrow could turn into cells with tumor like traits. Here they mapped the gene shifts behind that change. Such maps are vital for safe use of stem cells in care.

By profiling the changed cells, they named the main gene and pathway shifts at work. The findings flag risks that clinics must screen for before transplants. They also show what to watch as cells are grown for long spans. That watch list can make stem cell cures safer for patients.
plos-pone-0001498:
Laura Forsberg White and Marcello Pagano published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on the 1918 flu pandemic. That pandemic was the most deadly outbreak of the last century. With fresh fears of a new pandemic, its spread rate was worth a fresh count. The team used records from towns in Maryland and from two ships with well logged outbreaks.

From those close records they gauged how fast the 1918 virus passed from person to person. A firm rate from real data beats a guess from broad counts. It lets planners test control plans against a proven hard case. The work thus serves both history and future readiness.
plos-pone-0001598:
Sricharan Bandhakavi and co-authors wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on yeast that resists a key drug. The drug rapamycin blocks the TOR path, a master growth switch in cells. Some yeast shrug the drug off. The team combined protein counts with gene tests to find how. They flagged a heat shock factor as a key player.

Switching that factor on both curbed resistance and dimmed TOR signals. That ties stress reply to growth control in a new way. TOR is a cancer drug target in people, so yeast clues carry weight. They may hint at how tumors dodge TOR drugs too.
plos-pone-0001698:
Jian Fu, Kathryn Fong, Alfonso Bellacosa, and their co-authors studied a tumor suppressor protein lost in lung cancer, in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. The protein is VILIP-1, part of a family of neuronal calcium sensors. In animal models it acts as a tumor suppressor, slowing cell growth, adhesion, and invasion in squamous cell carcinoma.

The team examined non-small cell lung carcinomas, the commonest lung cancers, to learn how VILIP-1 is turned down and whether its level predicts survival. The full text gives the tumor cell tests, the mechanisms of downregulation they found, and the survival analysis. A protein whose loss marks worse outcomes could guide prognosis, and restoring it is a possible treatment idea.
plos-pone-0001798:
Jonghwan Kim, Ji-hoon Lee, and Vishwanath R. Iyer mapped the target genes of a cancer-linked protein across the genome in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Myc is a transcription factor involved in many human cancers, and its overexpression is tied to malignant transformation. In normal cells Myc rises with growth signals and in turn regulates downstream genes.

Their global identification of Myc targets reveals a direct role in mitochondrial biogenesis, the building of new mitochondria. It also details how Myc uses its DNA binding motif in living cells. The full text gives the target list and validation tests. A growth switch that also orders more power plants explains part of how Myc fuels tumor growth.
plos-pone-0001898:
Branwen Hennig and co-authors asked why genes shape the response to the hepatitis B vaccine, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. The vaccine is safe and works well, yet the level of protective proteins it raises fades with time. A high peak right after the shots means a slower fade and a lower risk of infection later.

The team looked for host gene traits that track with that peak level and with how fast it falls. Knowing which traits matter could help spot people who need extra shots. It also shows how much of vaccine success is set by the person, not just the dose. Such work can guide smarter vaccine plans.
plos-pone-0001998:
Pedro Martins, Fernando Rocha, and Ana Damas studied the physics of growing protein crystals, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. To read a protein's shape, labs grow crystals of it, most often by vapor diffusion: a drop loses water slowly until crystals form. The rate at which water leaves the drop sets the quality of the crystals.

Past attempts to solve the math of that evaporation, by formula or by numbers, left gaps. The trio set out the basics of how water balance is reached in the setup. A rational grasp of the step could replace trial and error with design in crystal growth.
plos-pone-0002098:
Kamran Shalchian-Tabrizi and co-authors used many genes to redraw the tree at the root of animals, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Animals are kin to fungi and to Choanozoa, mostly one-celled protozoans, in a great group called opisthokonts. To set the order of events when animals evolved from one-celled ancestors, the branches closest to that split must be right.

The team built a multigene phylogeny of Choanozoa and its kin. Many genes together can settle branches that single genes leave shaky. Knowing which living groups are animals' closest kin shows what the first animals inherited, and what they invented.
plos-pone-0002198:
Jason Rasgon proposed a new way to tell what a mosquito has fed on, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. A mosquito that drinks blood can pass on malaria, dengue fever, and other diseases. Knowing which animals its blood came from helps trace how those diseases spread, but digestion destroys the meal fast. Current tests only work soon after feeding.

Rasgon suggests stable isotope analysis, which reads lasting chemical signatures in the mosquito's tissues. Those signatures can survive complete digestion of the blood meal. If the method holds up, disease teams could learn the feeding habits of caught mosquitoes long after the evidence would once have vanished.
plos-pone-0002298:
Jonathan FitzGerald, Ming Luo, and Abed Chaudhury tested a prediction about parent conflict in plant seeds, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. The parental conflict idea says a mother plant restrains embryo growth while the father pushes it up, each serving their own genetic interest. In plants, the enzyme MET1, which places methyl marks on DNA, is a central regulator of the imprinted genes that tune seed growth.

The team asked how DNA methylation links the two parents' opposing pressures to actual embryo size. Their results show methylation causes predominantly maternal control of plant embryo growth. The finding refines how genetic conflict in seeds is understood at the molecular level.
plos-pone-0002398:
A research team led by Martin reported its work in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline credits Bronwen Martin, Michele Pearson, Randall Brenneman, and others. Its subject is conserved and Differential Effects of Dietary Energy Intake on the Hippocampal Transcriptomes of Females and Males. The level of dietary energy intake influences metabolism, reproductive function, the development of age-related diseases, and even cognitive behavior.

Key terms are set out in context, so a reader new to the field can still follow the work. The full text is free to read, so any reader can check the work and follow the links to past work.
plos-pone-0002498:
Work from Hwang and fellow authors appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline credits Nathaniel S. Hwang, Shyni Varghese, Jennifer Elisseeff, and others. Its subject is derivation of Chondrogenically-Committed Cells from Human Embryonic Cells for Cartilage Tissue Regeneration. Heterogeneous and uncontrolled differentiation of human embryonic stem cells (hESCs) in embryoid bodies (EBs) limits the potential use of hESCs for cell-based therapies.

Readers get the background first, then the path the team took and the care they took with it. That makes the article a clear record of one research question, the path taken to test it, and the limits the authors faced.
plos-pone-0002598:
In 2008, Valenzuela and colleagues published a study in the journal PLOS ONE. The byline credits Michael J. Valenzuela, Perminder Sachdev, Wei Wen, and others. Its subject is lifespan Mental Activity Predicts Diminished Rate of Hippocampal Atrophy. Epidemiological studies suggest that complex mental activity may reduce the risk for dementia, however an underlying mechanism remains unclear.

Key terms are set out in context, so a reader new to the field can still follow the work. The result is a compact record of the work, of use to readers who study the same problem or teach it to others.
plos-pone-0002698:
Published in PLOS ONE in 2008, research by Sun-Chong Wang and colleagues addresses Age-Specific epigenetic drift in Late-Onset alzheimer's disease. The catalog record names Sun-Chong Wang first among the authors, and the source is the open journal PLOS ONE.

The abstract begins from a clear premise. Despite an enormous research effort. For readers, the value lies in how plainly the abstract sets out the problem and what the authors set out to test or describe. No results or figures are claimed in this summary beyond what the title and abstract themselves state.
plos-pone-0002798:
Paolo Facella led a team whose work appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was diurnal and circadian rhythms in the tomato transcriptome and their modulation by cryptochrome photoreceptors. Authorship is credited in the record to Paolo Facella and co-authors, with PLOS ONE as the journal of publication.

The abstract begins from a clear premise. Circadian clocks are internal molecular time-keeping mechanisms that provide living organisms with the ability to adjust their growth and physiology and to anticipate diurnal. Its abstract frames the work for later readers, who can judge the full text against the aims stated at the start.
plos-pone-0002898:
Claudia Rübe, Jan Palm, Michael Erren and colleagues asked in 2008 whether blood cytokine levels can predict lung injury after radiation. Radiation is the main treatment for advanced lung cancer that cannot be removed by surgery. Its most serious dose-limiting harm is radiation pneumonitis, an inflammation of the lung.

Earlier reports had suggested that cytokine signals in plasma might flag who is at risk. The PLOS ONE paper tests that promise with a question in its title and data behind it. If such a test worked, doctors could tailor dose and watch high-risk patients more closely.
plos-pone-0002998:
Veronika Butin-Israeli, Dotan Uzi, Mahmoud Abd-El-Latif and co-authors used empty virus shells to protect mouse kidneys in 2008. Viruses trigger host defense and survival pathways during infection, but using real viruses for therapy is hampered by their harmful effects. SV40 capsids without DNA offer the trigger without the genome.

These DNA-free particles induced stress responses, survival pathways, and a pause in apoptosis, the authors report. Mice were protected from acute renal failure. Published in PLOS ONE, the approach tries to borrow a virus's alarm signals while leaving its dangers behind. Its full text, with tables and references, is openly available to any reader online.
plos-pone-0003098:
Gilberto Paz-Filho, Talin Babikian, Robert Asarnow and co-authors reported leptin treatment improving cognitive development in 2008. Leptin changes brain structure, neuron excitability, and synaptic plasticity, and it regulates feeding circuits. Its effects on how a child's learning and thinking develop were unknown.

Leptin replacement improved cognitive development, the title states, in the case or cases studied. Published in PLOS ONE, leptin deficiency is rare but revealing: a hormone known for satiety also shapes the developing mind. The finding widens what replacement therapy should be assessed for. Its full text, with tables and references, is openly available to any reader online.
plos-pone-0003198: Binh An Diep and colleagues published a PLOS ONE study in 2008 on a toxin in community MRSA, the drug-resistant staph bacterium spread outside hospitals. The title states its subject: what part Panton-Valentine leukocidin plays in how this bacterium causes disease. No abstract text beyond the title was supplied, so this record states no findings.
plos-pone-0003298:
Christopher D. Fiorillo proposes a general theory of neural computation in this single-author 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Although there has been tremendous progress in understanding the mechanics of the nervous system, there has not been a general theory of its computational function. The author presents a theory that relates established biophysical properties of single generic neurons to principles of computation.

The theory is based on prediction by single neurons, as the title states. Readers get an attempt to ground brain computation in what one neuron can do, rather than in abstract networks alone. Single neuron prediction, if right, would simplify many models of learning.
plos-pone-0007398:
Wen-feng Shi, Melanie Leong, Ellen Cho, and colleagues studied a grape compound's effect on prostate cancer signals in 2009. Resveratrol has well established chemopreventive effects on prostate cancer in earlier studies. The androgen receptor plays pivotal roles in prostate tumor growth, because these tumors depend on male hormone signaling to grow.

The exact molecular mechanisms linking resveratrol to the receptor were not fully explained. The authors examine repressive effects of resveratrol on androgen receptor transcriptional activity. Their PLOS ONE work tests whether the compound quiets hormone-driven gene programs. That mechanism could support prevention strategies.
plos-pone-0007498:
Jean Ndjomou and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on hepatitis C virus and the cell signals it lives with. Viruses exploit host machinery to multiply. One signaling chain, called MEK/ERK, helps many RNA viruses copy themselves. Whether it helps or hinders hepatitis C was unclear. The team blocked the pathway and watched what the virus did.

Blocking MEK/ERK boosted hepatitis C replication and virus output, the opposite of the usual pattern. So this virus relates to the host's signaling in its own way. A pathway that restrains hepatitis C is a gift for drug thinking. Strengthening that restraint might slow the virus. The surprise also warns against assuming all RNA viruses treat host signals alike. Each virus negotiates its own deal with the cell.
plos-pone-0007598:
Inna Djagaeva and Sergey Doronkin published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 that follows their earlier work on how neurons shape their branches. The COP9 signalosome is part of the cell's protein degradation system. Its components are altered in patients with several severe syndromes, hinting at a role in neural circuits. The team asked how COP9 controls dendritic branching in fruit fly neurons. Their trail led to a protein called Kelch.

Kelch crosslinks the actin skeleton inside growing branches. COP9 limits branching by ordering Kelch's destruction through a Cullin3-dependent pathway. Controlled removal of a crosslinker prunes growth to the right extent. The mechanism links general protein recycling to precise brain wiring. It also gives the earlier, broader observations a concrete molecular story. One named protein's disposal explains how a neuron keeps its arbor in bounds.
plos-pone-0007698:
Claudia Tortiglione and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It concerns Hydra, a tiny freshwater animal with a simple body. Tiny glowing crystals called fluorescent nanocrystals can be tracked as they move through living tissue. Researchers value them as carriers and probes.

The team watched where the crystals entered Hydra's cells and how they passed between them. Entry turned out to be controlled, through regulated portals rather than random leaks. Knowing how cells take in such particles matters for drug delivery. It also matters for judging the safety of engineered particles.
plos-pone-0007798:
Qunzhou Zhang and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It studies stem-like cells taken from keloids, overgrown scars unique to human skin. Changes in a stem cell's local niche can push growth toward tumors. Whether a niche can drive a benign growth was unexplored.

Keloid cells turned out to be governed by their inflammatory niche. Two signals, IL-17 and IL-6, form the axis that drives them. The keloid thus serves as a model of niche-driven growth without cancer. Understanding that axis could lead to treatments that calm the niche rather than cut the scar out.
plos-pone-0007898:
Paul Bangirana and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It asks what predicts thinking skills in Ugandan children. Many programs aim to improve cognition in at-risk children. To guide them, researchers must first find the key variables that predict cognitive performance.

The team measured socioeconomic factors alongside children's cognition. Household wealth, schooling and related factors emerged as predictors. The study was designed to point community interventions at what matters most. Its implications reach beyond Uganda. Where resources are scarce, knowing which levers work is the first step to helping children think and learn better.
plos-pone-0007998:
Caroline Bidon and colleagues fed a plant extract to rats losing muscle with age, in PLOS ONE in 2009. The extract, EGb 761, comes from ginkgo leaves and is sold as a supplement. Muscle loss in old age, called sarcopenia, raises the risk of falls and lost independence.

In the rats' worn muscles, the extract woke a gene pattern more like that of young muscle. The shift was broad, across many genes at once, rather than a single change. The result hints that the extract reprograms aging muscle, though proof in people would need its own trials.
plos-pone-0008098:
Lulin Huang and colleagues read the silkworm's whole gene answer to a killer germ in PLOS ONE in 2009. The germ, whose name in the record reads Bacillus bombyseptieus, makes spores and poison crystals and was first found in dead silkworms. Silk farms lose whole batches to it.

Genome-wide reads showed which silkworm genes wake, and which go quiet, as infection takes hold. That full answer sheet reveals the insect's defense plan in detail. Breeders can use it to raise hardier worms, and the plan may echo in other insects facing kindred germs.
plos-pone-0008198:
Jeanette C. Perron and Jane Dodd studied cell movement signals in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. Bone morphogenetic proteins, or BMPs, can steer cells toward a source. This steering, called chemotaxis, starts fast at the cell surface. It likely uses paths apart from the slower gene-based responses to BMP. The team focused on BMP7.

They asked which receptor parts BMP7 needs to trigger this movement. Two subunits, ActRIIA and BMPRII, proved selectively required. The response also worked without Smad4, a usual BMP partner. The findings separate rapid steering signals from classic BMP signaling.
plos-pone-0008298:
Orie T. Shafer and Paul H. Taghert studied a clock neuropeptide in fruit flies in PLOS ONE in 2009. Neuropeptide signaling is a key part of circadian timekeeping in animals. Pigment dispersing factor, or PDF, is required for normal daily activity rhythms in Drosophila. Where in the brain PDF acts for each function was unknown. The team used RNA interference to knock it down in neuron subsets.

Silencing PDF in specific neuronal groups separated its various circadian roles. That maps anatomy onto function for this neuropeptide. Knowing which neurons do what sharpens models of the body clock. The approach can be reused for other clock signals.
plos-pone-0008398:
Daniel Shriner and colleagues tested height genetics across populations in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. Human height is the classic polygenic trait, shaped by many genes. Recent studies found variants influencing adult height. Those studies mainly involved East Asian or European ancestry groups. Whether the same loci transfer to other populations was open.

The team examined many variants representing over a hundred loci across populations. Fine-mapping can narrow which variant truly drives each signal. Transferability matters for applying genome findings worldwide. The study checks that genome discoveries do not stay confined to one ancestry.
plos-pone-0008498:
Koichi Iijima and co-authors study energy control in fruit flies in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. A factor called CREB helps control sugar and fat stores. In mammals, CREB acts in fat tissue and liver. Flies have a matching factor called dCREB2. Its role in energy metabolism was not fully known. The team switch CREB activity on or off in specific fly tissues.

They find both neuronal and peripheral CREB activity shape energy stores. Activity in the brain and in body tissues affects feeding too. The split shows energy balance is not run from one place. Fly work thus mirrors the multi-tissue control seen in mammals.
plos-pone-0008598:
Xinwei Chen and co-authors analyze barley resistance to leaf rust in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Barley leaf rust is caused by the fungus Puccinia hordei. Genetic resistance involves both major R genes and quantitative trait loci. R genes give higher but less durable resistance. Quantitative loci give partial resistance that lasts longer in the field. Exploring that partial resistance has become a breeding priority. The team use an eQTL analysis, linking gene expression to trait loci.

Their analysis maps expression loci behind partial resistance to the fungus. Genes whose expression varies with resistance become candidates. Breeders can use those markers to select durable resistance. The approach merges genetics and gene expression for crop improvement.
plos-pone-0008698:
Wendy Imlach, Sarah Finch, John Miller, and colleagues tested whether a potassium channel helps set heartbeat pace. Their rodent study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Heart cells fire in rhythm thanks to channels that pass charged particles. Large channels known as BK channels were known in many tissues. Their part in pacing the heart was unclear.

The researchers studied rodents with changes in these channels. They watched heart rate and how it answers bodily demands. The results give BK channels a real share in rate control. That finding adds a piece to the puzzle of rhythm faults and may guide future heart drugs.
plos-pone-0008798:
Mei Qiang, Ashley Denny, Jiguo Chen, and colleagues linked alcohol exposure to a removed chemical tag in brain genes. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. The NMDA receptor is a key target of alcohol in the brain. Repeated alcohol bouts raise production of its 2B subunit for a long time. Tag-based gene control, called epigenetic regulation, was suspected. Methyl tags near a gene usually keep it quiet.

After chronic intermittent ethanol, one spot near the 2B gene lost its methyl tag. Gene activity rose at the same time. Site-specific tag loss may lock in alcohol's brain changes. That mechanism could matter for addiction's persistence.
plos-pone-0008898:
Juan Nunez-Iglesias, Chun-Chi Liu, Todd Morgan, and colleagues profiled two RNA layers together in Alzheimer brains. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. MicroRNAs fine-tune how much protein each gene message makes. Their role in Alzheimer disease was little studied. Single-layer studies miss how the tuners and their targets move together. Brain cortex samples from patients offered both layers at once.

Joint profiling showed altered microRNA regulation across the cortex. Some messages rose exactly where their tuner RNAs fell. Paired patterns nominate real regulatory pairs for testing. Dementia research gains a richer map of gene control gone wrong.
plos-pone-0008998:
Frank Curriero and co-authors offered a fix for health records that lack a usable address, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Health research often maps where patients live to spot disease patterns. Mapping needs each record's location pinned down, a step called geocoding. Some addresses cannot be matched to a map, and those records are usually dropped.

The team used imputation, a statistical fill-in method, for the missing locations. Instead of discarding unmatched records, they estimated where those patients likely lived. Keeping the records avoids biasing the map toward easy-to-place addresses. The approach widens the share of health data that mapping studies can honestly use.
plos-pone-0009098:
Lokesh Gakhar and co-authors introduced an airway protein that fights germ films, in PLOS ONE in 2010. PLUNC is a protein poured out by the lining of the human airways. It belongs to a family that handles fats and bacterial toxins. Its exact job in the lung was unsettled.

The team showed PLUNC acts like a surfactant, lowering surface tension. It also attacked biofilms, the slimy cities bacteria build on surfaces. Biofilms protect germs in chronically infected lungs. An airway protein that breaks them up could inspire new lung treatments.
plos-pone-0009198:
Samir Koirala and Gabriel Corfas published this brain study in PLOS ONE in 2010. It profiles Bergmann glial cells, support cells in the cerebellum, the brain region that fine-tunes movement. While young, these cells guide migrating neurons into place. In adults, they help form the cerebellum's outer boundary and support its wiring.

Despite their importance, many genes active in Bergmann glia were unknown. The team read the gene activity of single cells taken from mouse cerebellum. That single-cell profiling turned up glial genes that had not been identified before. The new gene list gives researchers fresh leads on how the cerebellum is built and kept working.
plos-pone-0009298:
Anne-Laure Leoni and co-authors published this heart mouse study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Faults in the gene SCN5A weaken a key heart channel, Nav1.5. Carriers can develop conduction disease or Brugada syndrome, but not always. The same fault leaves some hearts nearly normal, a puzzle called variable penetrance.

The team used mice carrying one faulty copy of the gene. They measured how much working channel protein the healthy copy produced. That amount varied, and it tracked with how severe the conduction disease was. When the good copy compensates strongly, the heart fares better, which helps explain the uneven inheritance.
plos-pone-0011398:
Olivier Thaunat and co-authors compared immune responses in 2010 between normal lymph tissue and the makeshift lymph tissue that forms inside chronically inflamed organs. When inflammation lasts for months, the body builds these extra immune hubs at the site of disease. Doctors see them in arthritis, thyroid disease, and transplanted organs, but how well they work was unclear.

The team found that responses launched from these extra hubs have distinct features that set them apart from responses in lymph nodes. Those differences help explain why local immunity in a sick organ can behave in unusual, sometimes harmful ways. The finding matters for transplant care and autoimmune disease, where such hubs may drive the very damage doctors are trying to stop. Targeting the hubs could become a treatment aim.
plos-pone-0011498:
Xiaoling Wang, Saiyu Hang, and Lisa Prazak overturned a textbook role in 2010: a supposed brake on gene copying can also boost it. NELF was known for pausing the copying machine shortly after it starts on a gene, holding many genes in a ready state. Working in the Drosophila embryo, the team tested what happens to gene activity when NELF is removed.

Instead of rising, activity at many genes fell, showing that NELF potentiates transcription in the living embryo. A factor that both pauses and promotes is not a contradiction but a tuning device, setting genes up for fast, controlled release. The flip from brake to accelerator warns against naming proteins by their first discovered job. Developmental biologists must now read NELF's role gene by gene and stage by stage, which is slower work but truer to the embryo.
plos-pone-0011598:
Mairi Hunter and co-authors studied the faulty protein behind cystic fibrosis in PLOS ONE in 2010. The disease is caused by defects in CFTR, a channel that moves salts across cell surfaces. Not every feature of the illness follows from poor salt transport, though, and lung inflammation is one stubborn puzzle.

The team tested whether healthy CFTR calms inflammation signals driven by a switch called NF-kB. Adding normal CFTR did damp those signals down. That suggests the healthy protein normally acts as a brake on inflammation, and losing that brake helps explain why lungs in cystic fibrosis stay inflamed and scarred.
plos-pone-0011698:
Pedro Olea, Patricia Mateo-Tomás and Ángel de Frutos tested a stats tool that ecologists use a lot, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The tool, called hierarchical partitioning, helps pick out likely causes from tangled data where many factors overlap. Its use in nature studies is growing because it pairs well with standard regression.

The authors set out to measure bias in the free public version of the tool. A steady lean one way would matter, since choices about land and wildlife are based on the tool's output. Their check gives field scientists a better sense of how far that output can be trusted.
plos-pone-0011798:
Celine Franckhauser and co-authors tracked a division-driving enzyme in human cells, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The enzyme cdc25C was the first of its family found essential for activating the complex that starts mitosis, the division of the cell's nucleus. When cdc25C becomes active, it gains phosphate tags on specific proline-linked sites.

The team found distinct pools of cdc25C carrying different tags on specific sites, localised differently in dividing cells. Zoned control like this helps time mitosis with precision. Sorting the pools clarifies how a single enzyme can serve several timed steps.
plos-pone-0011898:
Linea Melchior and colleagues analyzed ancient DNA in 2010 from ninety-two people buried in Denmark between the Mesolithic and the medieval age. Mitochondrial DNA, passed down the maternal line, was recovered from eighteen locations. Strict rules for fossil DNA work were applied, and clear maternal haplotypes could be assigned for fifty-six of the individuals.

The spread of those lineages across thousands of years shows how genetically varied early Nordic populations were. Such data test whether today's Danes descend mostly from Stone Age locals or from later arrivals who replaced them. Ancient bones answer that question directly, in a way written records from the period cannot.
plos-pone-0011998:
Johan Lindgren, Michael Caldwell, and Takuya Konishi drew in 2010 on an exceptional mosasaur fossil to rethink how giant sea lizards swam. Mosasaurs were lizards that returned to the sea and radiated during the late Cretaceous. They were long pictured as simple eel-like swimmers, wriggling their whole bodies.

The fossil's preserved features point to a more advanced swimming style, closer to that of fast modern swimmers. That is convergent evolution: unrelated lineages arriving at the same solution for moving through water. A single well-preserved animal can overturn a family-wide assumption, and this one recasts mosasaurs as more capable cruisers than their old image allowed.
plos-pone-0012098:
Valeria De Arcangelis, Filippo Serra, Carlo Cogoni, and colleagues studied muscle disease in mice for PLOS ONE in 2010. The mice lack a key muscle protein, like boys with the muscle-wasting illness this strain models. Without it, a whole group of support proteins in the muscle fiber also fades away, leaving fibers weak and easy to damage.

The team focused on one small RNA that can dial down a support protein in that group. Their work links the rise of this small RNA to the loss of its target in sick muscle. That kind of link matters because small RNAs can be blocked with drugs, raising a possible path to protect muscle fibers.
plos-pone-0012198:
Jonathan Chen, Ka-Hing Wong, Zhiwei Chen, and co-authors tracked the changing mix of HIV strains in Hong Kong for PLOS ONE in 2010. HIV falls into subtypes and blended recombinant forms that differ by region, and new blends had been appearing in the city with rising complexity. Their study set out to characterize what is actually circulating there.

They found the virus population growing more genetically diverse over time. Rising diversity complicates everything from blood screening to vaccine design, since a test or shot tuned to one strain may miss another. Cities that track their strains early can update clinics and prevention programs before the mix outruns them.
plos-pone-0012298:
Gerald Herrera and Andrea Meredith charted the daily rhythm of bladder function in rats, in PLOS ONE in 2010. People store urine at night and void mostly by day, a pattern so familiar it is rarely questioned. Animal models of bladder disease, though, had never been carefully checked for the same daily swing, which could quietly distort experiments run at one time of day.

Their measurements establish how the rat bladder's storage and voiding change across the day. With that baseline, bladder studies can be scheduled and compared honestly, and diseases that break the rhythm, like nighttime urination in older people, gain a workable model. Sometimes the most useful paper is the one that measures the obvious properly.
plos-pone-0012398:
Norman Baker, Samantha Zeitlin, Linda Shi and co-workers studied what happens when chromosome tips break during cell division, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Cells guard their DNA with sensors that fix damage, but during division those systems work differently and are less understood. The team damaged chromosome ends while cells were in the final split stage, called anaphase.

They found that broken tips at that late stage block the cell from finishing cytokinesis, the pinch that separates two new cells. The block likely stops damaged DNA from passing to daughter cells. Understanding such last-minute brakes helps explain how cells avoid the unstable genomes that seed cancer.
plos-pone-0012498:
Ada Delaney, Margaret Keighren, Susan Fleetwood-Walker and colleagues studied a pigment gene's role in pain, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. The melanocortin-1 receptor is famous for setting red hair and fair skin, but it also sits in pain pathways and varies between people. The team asked which kinds of pain this receptor actually shapes.

Their tests showed the receptor matters for acute pain and for pain from inflammation, but not for neuropathic pain after nerve injury. Splitting pain types matters for drug design, since a blocker that helps inflamed joints may do nothing for nerve pain. Genetic pain profiling starts with such distinctions.
plos-pone-0012598:
Lingappa, Hughes, Wang and co-authors asked a practical question about HIV spread between sexual partners. The amount of HIV in a person's blood is closely tied to how likely they are to pass the virus on. Their 2010 paper estimates how much that risk falls when blood virus levels drop.

The team built a numeric estimate linking virus level in blood plasma to the chance of transmission to a partner. Such an estimate matters for prevention, because drugs that lower virus levels may also cut spread. Their figures help planners judge how much treatment can slow the epidemic.
plos-pone-0012698:
Hartbauer, Ofner, Grossauer and co-authors asked whether singing bushcrickets carry a backup alarm for bat attacks. A male's loud song draws females, yet the same sound can guide hunting bats to him. Their 2010 study looked at the cercal organ, a small sense organ at the rear of these insects.

They propose this organ may detect bats that the main ears miss, giving the singer a last warning. A backup sense would change how we read the arms race between singing insects and bats. The idea also shows how much sensing fits into a small body.
plos-pone-0012798:
Ball, Field and Tippins showed that chemical stress can make the thromboxane receptor more dangerous. Thromboxane A2 is a short-lived signal that tightens blood vessels and drives clotting. Its receptor sits at the centre of normal vessel tone control, and faults feed heart attacks and strokes.

Their 2010 study found oxidative stress steadies the receptor, moves it, and makes it answer more strongly. Three changes at once explain how stressed vessels can overreact. The result ties everyday oxidative stress to a concrete vessel control fault.  Vessel behaviour was tested in living artery tissue.
pmc-11223798:
Pang, Lu, Zhou, and co-authors introduce MetaboAnalyst version six, a single platform for metabolomics work. Metabolomics studies the small molecules found in cells, blood, and other samples. The platform handles data from both focused tests and broad scans, mainly those using liquid methods paired with mass measurement.

Two goals drove the new version, the authors say: join steps that once sat in separate tools, and make results easier to read. Processing, analysis, and interpretation now sit in one place. For labs, a unified workflow saves time and cuts errors when moving data between programs.
pmc-2265698:
Aziz, Bartels, Best, and co-authors describe the RAST Server for automatic annotation of microbial genomes. Genome sequences from bacteria and their relatives were arriving faster than experts could label them by hand. Annotation means naming each gene and guessing its role.

RAST offers a fully automated service that finds protein-coding genes, RNA genes, and more. It assigns functions using a subsystem approach that groups genes by the cell jobs they serve. Fast, consistent labelling lets small teams start biological analysis at once instead of spending months on setup.  Genome centres used the service to keep pace with sequencing output.
pmc-3772798:
Gupta, Kapoor, Chaudhary, and co-authors present a computational approach for predicting the toxicity of peptides and proteins. Research over past decades had focused on peptide and protein-based therapies for many diseases. Peptides offer advantages over small molecules, including high specificity, good penetration, and ease of manufacture.

A therapy must also be safe, and lab toxicity testing is slow and costly. Their in silico approach predicts harmful peptides before synthesis, guiding design toward safer candidates. Computer screening helps focus animal and cell testing on the most promising molecules.  Virtual screening first lets chemists reserve wet testing for a shortlist of candidates.
pmc-5015598:
The Early Breast Cancer Trialists' Collaborative Group, with McGale, Taylor, and others, analyzed radiotherapy after mastectomy in 2014. Earlier combined analyses showed that radiotherapy after mastectomy cuts recurrence and breast cancer death in women with node-positive disease overall. The benefit was uncertain for women whose cancer had reached just one, two, or three lymph nodes.

The team pooled individual patient data from many randomized trials, covering thousands of women. They measured effects on recurrence over ten years and breast cancer mortality over twenty years. Clear answers for the one-to-three node group matter because radiotherapy has real side effects. The analysis helped oncologists decide which women gain enough to justify treatment.
pmc-5705698:
Kyoko Watanabe, Erdogan Taskesen, Arjen van Bochoven, and colleagues introduced the FUMA web tool in 2017. Genome-wide association studies find DNA regions linked to traits, but most hits sit outside genes. Turning a list of hits into likely causal genes is a hard step.

FUMA lets users upload study results and map them to genes using position, gene activity data, and chromosome shape data. It also annotates the variants and tests which tissues and gene sets stand out. The tool runs in a browser with no coding needed. It has become a routine first step for interpreting association results.
pmc-6467998:
Tian Ge, Chia-Yen Chen, Yang Ni, and coauthors presented PRS-CS for polygenic prediction in 2019. Polygenic scores add up many small genetic effects to estimate disease risk. Better math can sharpen those scores without new data.

PRS-CS infers the true effect of each variant using association summaries plus a reference map of variant correlation. Its Bayesian shrinkage adapts to how heritable and complex a trait is. In tests it beat common rivals across several traits. Sharper scores help research on shared causes and, in time, may guide screening for high-risk groups.
pmc-8546498:
Veronika Skrivankova and colleagues published guidance in 2021 on how to report a kind of study that uses genes to test cause and effect. The method is called Mendelian randomisation. It treats the gene variants a person is born with as a kind of natural trial, which can show whether a habit or trait truly causes a health outcome. Reports of such studies, though, often leave out key facts.

This paper explains a reporting checklist for the method, item by item. It shows what good reporting looks like and warns where authors tend to cut corners. Clear reports matter here, because the results can shape advice on food, drugs, and daily habits. The checklist gives authors and reviewers one shared standard to work from.
plos-pone-0359598:
Haiou Cao and colleagues worked in 2026 on pinpointing the exact moment an electrical fault begins in an active distribution network. Knowing the fault inception time precisely helps engineers reconstruct what happened and how protection equipment behaved.
