Their method combines a distance measure between signals with Gaussian filtering, a smoothing technique, to sharpen that timing.

Modern local grids, with solar panels and batteries feeding in, behave less predictably than the one way networks of the past, so fault analysis tools must keep up. A method that stamps the start of a fault with high precision can shorten outages and improve the settings of protective relays. The study contributes to the quiet engineering that keeps neighborhood power dependable.
plos-pone-0359798:
Xiaoge Zhang, Xiaoyun Wang, Na Li, Qunying Han, and Zhengwen Liu published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It concerns advanced hepatocellular carcinoma, the most common type of liver cancer. The authors examine a group of drugs called 5-hydroxytryptamine 3 receptor antagonists, often used against nausea, and their link to patient prognosis.

To make the comparison fair, the team used propensity score matching, which pairs similar patients who did or did not receive these drugs. That design tries to separate the drug's association from other differences between patients. Oncologists may find the result useful when supportive-care drugs are chosen for people with advanced liver cancer.
plos-pone-0360098:
Carlos Gonzalez-Lopez, Adrian Overly, Saahil Singh, Charlie Huang, and Gabriel Lopez published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It describes a modular toolkit for building synthetic auxotrophs, microbes engineered to need a supplied chemical to live. Here that chemical is theophylline, a drug-like compound.

The control switch is a riboswitch, a piece of RNA that turns a gene on or off when it senses the chemical, gating genes the microbe cannot live without. Tying survival to a supplied compound is a safety strategy for engineered organisms. Synthetic biologists can reuse the kit's parts to build contained microbes for research or production.
plos-pone-0329598:
Morteza Jafari Malali, Sepideh Zolfaghari, and Raheleh Davoodi published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It works on EEG emotion recognition, teaching computers to read feelings from brain waves. Their method uses multilevel entropy analysis, measuring disorder in the signal at several levels, summed up in the title's phrase about the entropy of entropy.

The entropy measures are drawn from phase dynamics, how the brain wave's cycles evolve. Emotion recognition from EEG could one day support mental health tools and adaptive technology, but signals are messy and personal. Signal processing researchers are the audience for a new feature family tested on this hard problem.
plos-pone-0347898:
Liu Liu, David Okech, and Anna Cody published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. Set in Eastern Sierra Leone, it studies which household and child traits appear alongside indicators of child trafficking, signs that a child may be trafficked for labor or other exploitation.

Trafficking hides inside ordinary fostering and work arrangements, so survey indicators are one of the few tools for measuring it. Knowing which households and children show the most indicators helps protection services focus visits and support. Child welfare agencies working in West Africa are the audience for this risk profile.
plos-pone-0357898: Ueda and seven co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on treating acute myeloid leukemia, a fast-growing blood cancer. They looked at which gene traits and clinical traits predict response to two drugs used together, azacitidine and venetoclax. The data came from a Japanese study program coded HM-SCREEN-Japan 02. Knowing who is likely to respond helps doctors pick the right therapy early for each patient.
plos-pone-0358798: de Anda-Jáuregui and seven co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on hospital strain in Mexico City during COVID-19. Rather than just counting patients, they treated demand as a complex system with linked parts. Surges in one area can strain staff, beds, and oxygen in others. Seeing those links helps city health leaders prepare for the next crisis before wards overflow.
plos-pone-0357798: Ning and one co-author published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on designing car doors. A door must look good and also protect people in a crash. Those two goals often pull against each other: sleek shapes can clash with strong beams. The team worked on an optimized design that weighs appearance and safety together. Their approach speaks to car makers balancing style and crash rules.
plos-pone-0358998:
Charles Bakolo leads a team of eight mapping flood danger in Nsanje District, Malawi, in a 2026 PLOS ONE study. The low lying district in the Lower Shire valley floods again and again, wrecking homes, crops, and roads, yet fine grained local risk maps have been scarce. The authors combined mapping data with a structured decision method to grade every part of the district.

They weighed five factors: land cover, rainfall, slope, distance to water, and elevation, drawing on satellite images, rain records, and terrain data. Land cover mattered most, rainfall second. The finished map shows danger rising from north to south, with one traditional authority area standing out as most exposed and more than fifteen hundred residents in high risk zones. District planners gain a concrete guide for settling, drainage, and evacuation priorities.
plos-pone-0359198:
Ge Cai leads a team of eight setting out a planned trial for a painful childhood neck condition, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Atlantoaxial rotatory subluxation twists the top neck joint and locks a child's head at an angle. Gentle hands on treatment is common, but solid trial evidence for adding structured muscle training is missing. The protocol also tests whether ultrasound stiffness measures can track recovery without radiation.

Seventy children aged two to eighteen will be assigned by chance to joint mobilization alone or mobilization plus neck resistance training, three sessions a week for four weeks. Ultrasound shear wave imaging will measure the stiffness of a key neck muscle, alongside pain, movement range, and recurrence. Assessors will not know which child got which treatment. The design aims to give clinicians firmer ground for a condition now treated largely by habit.

plos-pone-0358698:
Izabela Hawro and three colleagues untangle who controls a liver nutrient cycle in mice, in PLOS ONE in 2026. The methionine cycle recycles an amino acid, and it falters in fatty liver disease, where a fat sensing switch called PPAR gamma rises in liver cells. The team asked whether that switch drives the cycle's gene changes across fasting, refeeding, and diet induced obesity, using mice whose liver cells lack the switch.

Fasting switched the cycle's genes up; a six hour refeed switched them back down. Removing the switch did not strengthen those swings, so the fasting rhythm is not the switch's doing. A drug that activates the switch turned two cycle genes down in obese mice. That effect depended on the switch being present. Control is split. Feeding rhythms run the cycle independently. The fat sensor can override it under drug pressure.
plos-pone-0356598:
Jieun Hwang and three colleagues studied alcohol-related disorders in Korea in a PLOS ONE paper from 2026. Mental and behavioral disorders caused by alcohol rarely come alone; other health problems cluster with them. The team used a national hospital discharge survey that also records injuries in depth.

Hwang's group mapped which other conditions most often appear beside alcohol-induced disorders. That map guides doctors toward whole-person treatment instead of chasing each diagnosis in isolation. Hospital planners can also see what combined services these patients need. For a group often treated in fragments across departments, evidence of clustering is a strong argument for integrated care pathways.
plos-pone-0347398:
Huajun Chen and three colleagues linked flying taxis, 6G networks, and carbon goals in a PLOS ONE paper from 2026. Electric vertical aircraft, called eVTOLs, will need dense wireless networks and charging systems to run a low-altitude economy. Running that support all day would waste energy and add emissions.

Chen's team proposed a sleep strategy for wireless charging setups, guided by how time, energy use, and carbon output interact. Parts of the system rest when skies are quiet, then wake for demand. Their aim is a low-altitude transport system that can grow without blocking carbon neutrality. The work joins two fields, aviation and telecom, that rarely plan together.
plos-pone-0357098:
Valeria Teso led a team of eight authors who surveyed a deep submarine canyon off Argentina, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Using a remotely operated vehicle, they explored the Mar del Plata Canyon in the southwestern Atlantic. Such canyons are rarely visited, which makes them good places to check how far human litter has spread.

Teso's survey revealed marine litter hidden in the deep canyon. Documenting trash at depth matters because the deep sea is often assumed clean by default. That assumption delays action. Evidence from the ROV gives waste policy a concrete picture. What people discard on land and at sea can end up in places almost no human will ever visit. There it may harm deep life for a very long time.
plos-pone-0357498:
Jia Sun led a team of eight authors studying a brain fluid structure near tumors, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. The choroid plexus makes cerebrospinal fluid, and its size can change in patients with gliomas and related brain tumors. The team measured that volume variation and linked it to tumor traits.

Sun's findings raise the chance that choroid plexus volume could serve as an imaging marker. Markers readable from standard scans are valuable because they add information without new tests. Tumor type, size, and behavior all guide treatment, so any extra signal helps planning. The study is early, but it directs attention to a structure radiologists often pass over when reading brain scans for tumors.
plos-pone-0354798:
Maryam Shahdoust and colleagues published a 2026 paper in PLOS ONE introducing ElecMeter, a new index for measuring voter dissatisfaction after a single-winner election. Most voting measures track satisfaction or total welfare, leaving the losing side's discontent unmeasured. ElecMeter instead scores an outcome by where the winner ranks in each voter's preference list. It also examines how dissatisfaction spreads across the electorate, setting it beside patterns of extreme discontent.

Simulations show the index can separate electorates that share the same average dissatisfaction but differ in how that discontent is distributed. On a classic food-preference dataset, it picked consistent winners across its settings and agreed with several long-standing voting rules. The authors publish their code and data openly. The index gives election researchers a way to diagnose acceptance and cohesion problems that satisfaction scores alone would miss.
plos-pone-0357598:
Tiantian Yao and coauthors published a 2026 spatial planning study in PLOS ONE on ecological sensitivity in the flat, crowded Yangtze River Delta in China. Most sensitivity research concerns mountains, leaving highly urbanized plains without guidance. In a cross-border green development zone, the team combined ten indicators, geography, water, resources, and human interference, through expert weighting and mapping software, then ranked what shapes sensitivity.

More than seventy percent of the zone rated medium to extremely high sensitivity, with the most fragile land clustered around its lakes and connected ecological areas, while built-up urban land rated lowest. Land use, night lights, population density, and closeness to water drove the pattern; slope and elevation barely mattered on the plain. New construction crept along city edges and roads, slicing sensitive belts and fragmenting core habitat. Zoning and corridor controls keyed to the sensitivity map are proposed for similar plains.
plos-pone-0355298:
Sangmi Lee examines when trusting other people protects young adults in Seoul from depression, and when it fails to. Social trust usually tracks with better mental health, yet the author suspected traditional views about men's and women's roles might blunt that protection. Survey data from several hundred adults aged nineteen to thirty-four were reanalyzed with a moderation model that accounted for gender, schooling, work status, and living arrangement.

Trust tied to lower depression overall, while traditional role attitudes tied to higher depression. The key result is the interaction: trust's link with lower symptoms held for young adults with low or average traditional attitudes and vanished among those with strongly traditional views. Lee suggests mental health programs in rapidly changing societies must reckon with values, not just connections.
plos-pone-0356498:
Maulana Malik and co-authors present an improved version of the conjugate gradient method, a workhorse algorithm for solving very large optimization problems where computing the full best answer directly is impossible. Their 2026 mathematics paper adds a third search term with a new descent structure, proves the method reliably moves downhill and settles at a solution under standard conditions, and then benchmarks it.

On standard test problems the new method reached answers faster than similar rival methods. The team also applied it to low-carbon supply chain planning, where companies balance cost against emissions. Faster, stabler optimization matters well beyond mathematics: the same machinery sits inside logistics planning, engineering design, and machine learning training.
plos-pone-0356398:
Mary Darking, Helen Ayles, and colleagues describe a youth-led design project in Zambia that built a digital sexual health service with the young people meant to use it. Their 2026 paper follows six stages, from recruiting youth co-design leaders to testing a working app, alongside a Zambian research partner, three European universities, and a nonprofit technology group.

Young participants mapped the whole journey, from picking up self-testing kits, partly through vending machines, to how lab results should reach a phone without exposing anyone. The result was a functional app plus a companion tool for clinic and lab staff, tested by the youth themselves. The project argues that designing in place, with users holding real authority, catches access barriers that outside designers miss.
plos-pone-0355198:
Alfonso Mendoza-Velázquez and colleagues tracked Mexican food prices from 2012 to 2025, asking whether healthy food became harder to afford through the pandemic years. Their 2026 study scored foods from a national dietary survey for nutrient density, sorted them by processing level, and linked both to official price series, modeling how inflation differed across categories.

Nutrient-dense, minimally processed foods were always far pricier per calorie than ultra-processed ones, which scored near zero for nutrient density. Inflation then hit the healthy basket hardest after the pandemic, widening the affordability gap even when percentage rises looked similar. The authors warn that identical inflation rates are not equal burdens when the nutritious starting point already costs more.
plos-pone-0356798:
Chiara Reck and colleagues reviewed the evidence for digital health programs at sea, where crews on cargo and passenger ships live with high stress and almost no access to ordinary health promotion. Their 2026 scoping review searched four databases systematically, screened nearly two thousand records down to sixty-eight full texts, and included just nine studies, plus a hunt for real-world programs already running.

The cupboard is nearly bare. The nine studies covered only cargo crews, mixed pilots with one proper trial, and split between behavior coaching, structural changes, and blends. Not one examined health literacy, the skill of finding and judging health information. For an industry that never comes ashore, the authors call digital prevention an obvious, unbuilt bridge.
plos-pone-0341298:
Abraham Aldama, Cristina Bicchieri, and Jana Freundt test a widely held belief about American politics in this 2026 study: that learning how unequal incomes really are will make people demand more redistribution. In a large survey experiment, they measured what Americans think people at the top and bottom earn, then corrected some participants' misperceptions and recorded their policy views and fairness judgments.

Americans turned out to underestimate pay at the bottom and overestimate pay at the top. Even so, correcting those beliefs changed nothing measurable. Support for redistribution, and political behavior more broadly, stayed put across income groups, party loyalties, and levels of trust in government. The authors conclude that information campaigns about inequality, on their own, are unlikely to shift what policies people want.
plos-pone-0355598:
Maria Tesfaye Gebeyehu and fellow researchers ran field trials to find the best planting pattern for fenugreek in northeastern Ethiopia. Fenugreek is a spice and medicinal crop that suits the local climate, yet few trials have tuned how it is sown. Their 2026 study tested five seed rates against three row spacings at two sites.

The best harvest came from the narrowest rows paired with a mid-high seed rate. The widest rows with the least seed gave the poorest harvest, at barely a third of the best. Gebeyehu and colleagues recommend the winning pairing for the district and similar areas. They also call for repeat trials across seasons and places before the advice is treated as final.
plos-pone-0356198:
Chen Cheng and co-authors studied how immune cells called macrophages interact with an aggressive breast cancer in three-dimensional culture. Triple-negative breast cancer often resists drugs, and macrophages inside tumours are part of that problem. Their 2026 work grew cancer cells into balls together with macrophages pushed toward two opposing states.

One macrophage state helped cancer cells survive, yet both states made the balls more sensitive to two standard chemotherapy drugs. Surprisingly, macrophages of both kinds lost their set identity in co-culture and drifted toward a mixed state. Gene analysis confirmed the blending. Cheng and colleagues say these shifting partnerships must be built into lab models that aim to predict treatment response.
plos-pone-0355698:
Xinyue Zhang and co-authors compared gut microbes and waste chemicals in people on long-term dialysis with healthy partners. Dialysis patients and their matched controls shared diet and living conditions, which sharpens the comparison. Their 2026 multi-centre study combined gene sequencing of stool microbes with chemical profiling of stool samples.

Microbe mixes differed clearly between groups, including shifts in two well-known gut genera. Nearly five hundred small chemicals also differed, clustering in amino acid, vitamin, fat, and related pathways. Five chemicals separated patients from controls well enough to serve as candidate markers. Links between one genus and several fat-related chemicals stood out. The authors say the paired data clarify how gut imbalance accompanies dialysis.
plos-pone-0355998:
Hua Guo and colleagues combined human beauty ratings with map-based visibility analysis to grade scenery in a Chinese geopark. Geoparks mix scientific value with tourism, but their landscapes vary too much for one simple scoring method. Their 2026 study of Longyan Global Geopark coupled survey-based scenic beauty scores with geographic information analysis.

Beauty scoring captured personal taste well but undervalued small or distant views. Visibility analysis supplied the missing spatial objectivity. The coupled model rated core scenic spots and mapped where quality runs high or low. Guo and colleagues offer the method as a transferable route for protecting valued views and planning visitor routes in mixed landscapes.
plos-pone-0354298:
Liangzhong Cao and co-authors show in 2026 how combining two kinds of satellite data can map winter wheat in a dry oasis area of northern Xinjiang. Radar and optical images from key growth stages supplied a large set of features, covering texture, colour, and change over time. A forest based method then picked the most useful features.

A small kept set, led by moisture sensitive bands and timing cues, mapped wheat with high accuracy. Spring months carried the most telling signals, when plants grow fast and head out. The mapped area came close to official records. Growers and officials could use such maps to track crop layout and risk.
plos-pone-0355498:
Samantha Kloft and co-authors check in 2026 whether a survey scale for trust in United States public health bodies measures what it claims. They focused on one part of the scale, covering belief that authorities act for the public good. Answers came from a national panel of more than two thousand adults, analysed with a method that judges each question on its own.

The full set held together well, but three negatively worded items gave almost no useful information and were cut. The shorter five item version stayed reliable and measured moderate to high trust more sharply. Older and more educated adults scored a bit higher on the refined scale.
plos-pone-0336198:
Maia Sieverding, Ahmad Addam, and Maya Al Farran run in 2026 a pilot trial of a women led community centre in Tripoli, north Lebanon, asking whether its sessions build social cohesion. Lebanese and Syrian women from nearby areas were assigned at random to be invited or not. Seven sessions mixed training with structured dialogue led by women volunteers.

Most invited women attended at least once. Participants gained in sense of belonging and in civic attitudes and actions, but general trust in others did not move, nor did several other measures. A short, light programme can shift some bonds, the authors conclude, while deeper trust may need longer work.
plos-pone-0355398:
Xulan Li led a team of nine authors on this 2026 comparison of coffee shops and teahouses in two Chinese cities, Qingdao and Jinan. Using yearly map data from 2018 to 2024 on a fine grid, they tracked how the two kinds of venues grew, mixed, and shifted across neighborhoods with different histories.

Coffee did not simply push tea out. Both cities saw growth, but venues clustered in select districts and blended in mixed-use areas, with clearer sorting by function in Qingdao. Li's results frame the change as uneven reshaping, useful for planners watching how daily habits and city districts change together.
plos-pone-0354898:
Yuan Wang and four colleagues published this 2026 computer vision paper on finding defects in power line insulators from drone photos. Damaged insulators can spark, flash over, or fail, but in aerial images the parts are tiny and backgrounds are cluttered. Their detector rebuilds a lightweight detection model with three swapped-in modules for richer scale and context handling.

The upgraded model caught more of the rare, awkward defect types that the base model missed. It stayed fast enough for live inspection work and grew only modestly in size. Wang's team sees it as a candidate for inspection gear that runs on modest onboard hardware.
plos-pone-0348698:
Tenisha Roos led a team of seven authors on this 2026 study of elephants returned to the wild after captivity in South Africa. Eleven rewilded African elephants on fenced reserves were watched for behavior and tested for stress hormones in dung, then compared with free-roaming elephants.

The rewilded animals behaved much like wild ones overall, with some clear differences in behavior and stress readings. The authors link those gaps partly to individual personality, since each elephant coped in its own style. Roos offers the findings to set honest expectations for future release projects.
plos-pone-0354698:
Erin C Blankenship-Sefczek led a team of six authors on this 2026 study of stress written into teeth. In a Mexican community with known health and nutrition records. Fifty-four teenagers had their first upper molars cast and examined for enamel lines that mark childhood stress during tooth formation, plus crown size and bump patterns.

Stress lines formed while the molar developed were tied to narrower spacing between the tooth's main bumps and weaker expression of a small extra bump, matching a leading model of tooth patterning. Molar shape shifts unpredictably under stress, the findings suggest.
plos-pone-0354198:
Dulce E Alarcón-Yaquetto and three colleagues published this 2026 systematic review of what type 2 diabetes costs depending on a patient's social position. They searched medical and economics sources for studies reporting treatment cost differences by education, income, job, residence, or ethnicity, then compared the ends of each social gradient.

People at the disadvantaged end used less care and racked up lower direct costs, and their lost work costs also ran lower, patterns suggesting unmet need rather than efficiency. Alarcón-Yaquetto warns that cheaper care for poorer patients may signal care they never received.
plos-pone-0354598:
Philipp Fuchs led a team of seven authors on this 2026 study of survival after cancer spreads to the choroid, the eye's blood-rich back layer. Seventy patients treated at one center between 2013 and 2025 were grouped by where their cancer began: lung, breast, or elsewhere. Imaging and records supplied tumor size and spread.

Older patients and those whose cancer had already seeded more than one other site died sooner, independently of other factors. Primary tumor type mattered less. Fuchs concludes youth and low overall spread, not the original cancer, best predict longer survival.
plos-pone-0353298:
Wang and colleagues, in a 2026 paper, build a hybrid model to guess how much charge is left in a lithium-ion battery. That number, called state of charge, guides electric cars and devices, yet it is hard to pin down because battery behavior bends and drifts over time. Guessing wrong can strand a driver or wear the battery out early.

Their model pairs two designs. A pyramidal attention part reads the battery's recent history at several time scales at once, from quick swings to slow trends. A memory network then tracks the long story and the quirks in between. Tested on battery data gathered at several temperatures, the hybrid beat six rival methods on error scores. The authors say the multi-scale reading is the key gain, and they offer the model for battery systems that must work in heat and cold alike.
plos-pone-0353698:
Binli Ma and five colleagues argue that in sepsis, the trend of a patient's white blood cells matters more than any single reading, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. Sepsis often depletes lymphocytes, the infection-fighting cells. Drawing on a large intensive care database, the team sorted more than sixteen hundred patients whose counts started low into four recovery trajectories, from steady rebound to stubbornly flat.

The flat group — about a third of patients — had the worst survival at four weeks and the highest death rates in intensive care and hospital. Early death, within a week, was not predicted by the pattern. If counts have not begun recovering by day three or four, the authors warn, the patient has entered the highest-risk state.
plos-pone-0349298: Domestic horses — recognizing unfamiliar predators from visual cues alone. This paper demonstrated it. The equine subjects distinguished threats they’d never met. The findings revealed innate predator templates — evolution’s warnings, hardwired.
plos-pone-0352998:
To and colleagues screened symptom-free adults in Vietnam for bowel growths in a 2026 study. Most local data came from people who already had gut symptoms, leaving the hidden rate in healthy-feeling adults unclear. Volunteers paid for their own scope exams at one center and answered questions on habits and family history.

Growths found ranged from small polyps to early cancers, grouped by how advanced they looked. The team tested which factors, such as age, weight, smoking, drinking, and family history, tracked with finding growths. Knowing the rate in people without symptoms helps doctors judge whether wider screening would catch disease early enough to justify its cost in Vietnam.
plos-pone-0353198:
Huang and colleagues tested Bermuda grass for protecting slopes of swelling soil in a 2026 study. Such soil shifts with water and shakes under traffic loads, weakening road edges. Planting grass at three densities, the team shook soil samples under varied pressure and frequency to mimic real loads.

Grass cut the slow build-up of deformation, and denser planting helped more. Grass also blunted the effect of squeezing pressure on soil stiffness. Roots binding the soil explain the steadier response. Living cover could thus serve two jobs at once: greener slopes and stronger ground beneath roads, at lower cost than hard engineering alone.
plos-pone-0352098:
Shiri introduced a software package for judging crop varieties across many trial sites in a 2026 paper. A variety that shines in one field may flop in another, so breeders need yield, stability, and risk judged together. The package uses a forest-based method that gives prediction ranges rather than single guesses.

Separate modules handle performance, stability, risk, and confidence ranges, with repeat sampling for honesty. Breeders can favor varieties with high average yield and low chance of very poor results. Risk-aware selection matters more as weather grows less predictable, and a ready package spreads the method beyond statisticians.
plos-pone-0353398:
Pouroushaninia and colleagues compared four bedside scores for predicting huge blood transfusions after injury in a 2026 study. Bleeding is a top cause of trauma death when recognized late. Records covered more than three hundred patients at a Tehran hospital who received at least one unit of blood over three years.

Scores based on pulse and blood pressure, exam signs, and lab-linked formulas were each tested for how well they separated patients who needed massive transfusion from those who did not. A clear winner helps emergency teams activate blood banks earlier. In busy trauma bays, a simple score that works beats a precise one that arrives too late.
plos-pone-0349598:
Alexander Blagojevic and four colleagues present this 2026 PLOS One engineering study on electrodes designed to connect with the nervous system. The devices are treated with a laser method that roughens their surface at several scales, which improves how well they carry signals. A drawback is that the finest surface features can be loosely attached and may break off during handling or surgery.

The researchers tested a cleaning step that blasts the surface with frozen carbon dioxide snow while the laser work is still in progress. Compared with ultrasonic cleaning, the snow method kept the surface stable while preserving more of the electrode's electrical performance, and it was faster. The team presents this as a step toward implants that keep working reliably inside the body.
plos-pone-0352598:
Bridget Hogg and seven co-authors set out this 2026 PLOS One protocol for COMBINA. COMBINA expands a proven European program against depression. The program works on four levels at once. It works through health workers, public awareness, community gatekeepers, and patients. In this project it will run for two years in five regions. The regions sit in Albania, Estonia, Greece, Ireland, and Spain. The program is tailored to groups at higher risk, like young people, migrants, and the long-term unemployed.

As a protocol, the paper describes design, not results. The five regions will be compared with matched control regions. Outcomes include suicide deaths, hospital stays for attempts, wellbeing, symptoms, and stigma. Willingness to seek help will be tracked too. Process and cost studies will run alongside. Materials were co-created with members of the at-risk groups. The authors detail how one model adapts across very different national settings.
plos-pone-0349698:
Chansun Park and five colleagues characterise radiation detectors for cancer treatment in this 2026 study. Modern radiotherapy needs dosimeters that are fast, precise, and small. Cadmium zinc telluride detectors look promising. Yet their behaviour under medical electron beams was poorly documented. The team tested two detectors of different thicknesses on a clinical treatment machine. Beam energies spanned the usual therapeutic range.

Both detectors responded in clean proportion to dose. Readings stayed steady across dose rates and over two months of use. Thickness created a trade-off. The thicker detector captured more energy from high-energy electrons. The thinner one answered more evenly from different beam angles. Small-field and point-dose work needs exactly this kind of detail. The results tell medical physicists which thickness suits which measurement job.
plos-pone-0350498:
Baymot Bekele and seven colleagues measure how much hospital patients trust their care providers in northwest Ethiopia. Their 2026 survey covers five public hospitals in the Awi Zone. Six hundred twenty-one inpatients on medical, surgical, and gynaecology wards answered interviewer-led questionnaires. Trust matters because it shapes whether people seek care and follow treatment. It had barely been studied in this setting before.

Just under half the patients reported high trust in providers. Rural patients trusted more than urban ones. Patients without other chronic illnesses also trusted more. Curiously, patients lacking health insurance reported higher trust as well. The middling overall level is the headline, though. Hospitals wanting stronger patient relationships now know which groups feel least confident. Efforts to build trust can start with urban and chronically ill patients, whose doubts run deepest.
plos-pone-0352198:
Jieun Shin, Yeon-Ju Baek, and Nam-Yi Kim analyse five years of patient fall reports from Korean hospitals. Their 2026 study uses the patient safety reporting system. Nearly thirty thousand fall incidents arrived between 2020 and 2024. Falls were sorted by how much harm followed, from near miss to sentinel event. The team asked which patients, hospitals, and circumstances predicted the harmful falls rather than the harmless ones.

Falls' share of all safety reports fell from fifty-six percent to about thirty-nine. Yet the number of reported falls kept rising, so reporting culture, not just danger, was shifting. Harmful falls struck older patients, especially past sixty, and women more often. Long-term care hospitals and very large hospitals carried elevated risk. Night-time and department patterns rounded out the risk picture. Prevention budgets follow such maps: the study shows exactly which wards and patients need rails, alarms, and watching first.
plos-pone-0350298:
Aurore Monnereau and colleagues read ancient DNA from medieval Sicily, an island ruled in turn by Byzantine, Arab, Norman, and Swabian powers. Churches and cemeteries there served several faiths, yet how much the island's people themselves changed with each regime was unknown. The team analyzed remains of more than a hundred people buried between the fifth and fifteenth centuries.

The genes told a story of mixing rather than replacement. Some people who died before the Islamic conquest already carried much North African ancestry, so movement across the sea predated it. Graves in Islamic cemeteries held people of varied Mediterranean ancestry, but similar mixes appear in earlier burials too. Faith and ancestry, the data suggest, did not map neatly onto each other.
plos-pone-0350098:
Dog owners and cat owners both say their animals ease stress, but Niwako Ogata, Anna L Heck, and Hsin-Yi Weng asked whether the paths differ by species. Their 2026 PLOS One paper drew on survey answers from roughly nineteen hundred dog owners and eighteen hundred cat owners, gathered during the COVID-19 pandemic.

Overall stress differed only slightly, with dog owners a touch lower. Daily hands-on interaction linked strongly to lower stress for dog owners but barely for cat owners, while emotional closeness mattered most for cat owners. Costs and behavior problems tracked with higher stress in both groups. Most of the gap remains unexplained, the authors note.
plos-pone-0351698:
A common gene variant in the FTO gene raises the odds of obesity, and Ingrid Løvold Mostad and colleagues wondered whether it changes the fats stored in body fat tissue. Their 2026 PLOS One study enrolled ninety-five adults with severe obesity and no diabetes, grouped by how many copies of the variant they carried.

Fat samples were drawn from belly and hip areas and their fatty acids measured in the lab. Across the whole group, the gene variant showed no clear link to any single fat. One difference in men rested on very small numbers, so the authors treat it with caution. Belly fat held more saturated fat than hip fat, regardless of genes.
plos-pone-0350698:
Health economists often model a disease as patients moving between health states over time, a method called Markov modeling. Jean Martial Kouame and colleagues wrote this 2026 PLOS One tutorial to show, in the free R software, how to let the odds of moving between states change as time passes.

A breast cancer example carries the lesson. Two fixes are demonstrated: making transition odds depend on time since the model started, and adding tunnel states that remember how long a patient has been ill. The tutorial also covers weighing costs against benefits, testing uncertainty, and valuing better information, giving analysts a full worked recipe.
plos-pone-0351498:
Dentures held by two lower jaw implants are a standard fix for people missing all lower teeth, and Burç İhsan Gencel and colleagues modeled how the holding parts spread chewing stress. Their 2026 PLOS One computer study compared snap-style locators with a connecting bar across three bone crest shapes.

A standard biting force was applied at the front, on one side, and on both back teeth. Front biting produced the highest stresses everywhere, peaking on rounded and uneven bone. Biting on both sides spread the load most evenly. Uneven bone under the denture raised stress notably. The results help dentists match attachment choice to a patient's jaw shape.
plos-pone-0344298:
Digital posters feel weightless, but servers, networks, and screens burn power to show them. Yilin Liu and Ping Ji measured the full life of digital poster systems, from design to deletion, in this 2026 PLOS One study following a marketing agency for six months.

Each unit of poster work carried a carbon cost of several kilograms. Delivery infrastructure and display time caused nearly nine tenths of the impact. Smarter hardware, showing posters at better times, and cloud platforms cut climate impact by almost a third. Data center efficiency mattered most of all. The authors offer the method so designers can count digital work honestly.
plos-pone-0351298:
Jananee Rasiah and colleagues described long term home care clients in Alberta, Canada, who live with frailty and use hospital care. Records linked more than ten thousand clients aged sixty five to over one hundred, followed from 2015 to 2017. Most clients were women, and the largest group was aged seventy five to eighty four.

Arthritis and high blood pressure were the most common added illnesses among frail clients. About four in ten frail clients visited emergency care one to three times, and hospital stays averaged over two weeks. Being pre frail or frail raised the odds of hospital admission. Social factors that push frail clients toward hospital, the authors note, still need mapping.
plos-pone-0350198:
Nang Kham-Kjing and colleagues searched for causes of severe lung infections in adults admitted to a hospital in Chiang Mai, Thailand, after the COVID pandemic. Swabs and spit from just over one hundred patients, admitted between late 2023 and spring 2024, were tested for twenty two respiratory viruses and one atypical germ with a combined lab test.

Just under half of patients tested positive for at least one germ. Adenovirus led, followed by rhinovirus, the common cold virus. About one in eleven patients carried more than one germ. Flu and rhinovirus peaked in January, while adenovirus and enterovirus lingered all season. Post pandemic virus patterns, the team shows, do not simply return to old norms.
plos-pone-0351398:
Ryo Asaoka, Shigeki Muto, and Akira Obana measured sugar damage build up in skin among just over sixteen hundred adults at health checks in Japan. Sugars that stick to proteins over years can harm kidneys, yet screening links were untested. Skin glow readings estimated build up without blood draws, and kidney function was estimated from standard labs. No one with known kidney disease was included.

Higher build up went with lower kidney function across the whole group, even among people whose kidney function still sat in the normal top band. The link held after other factors were counted. Whether the build up causes kidney decline or merely marks it stays open, but a quick skin reading may flag early risk.
plos-pone-0346698:
Pilar Montero-Alía and colleagues in Spain set out a study plan in 2026 for counting balance disorders in older adults. Poor balance leads to falls, and falls can end a person's independence, yet good population figures are scarce. No results are reported yet.

About thirteen hundred residents of Mataró aged in their late sixties and early seventies will take balance tests, some on a force platform and some on a home game board. Eye scans, leg strength, and a combined health score will also be checked. Follow-up after about eighteen months will show how often new balance problems appear and what predicts them.
plos-pone-0345098:
Dong Pan, Zhewen Lu, and Ye Yan evaluated a cleanup of the rules a computer system uses to check antibiotic prescriptions before they are filled at a county hospital in China. Reviewers tightened the rule set around the most common problems in outpatient prescriptions. Prescriptions written before the cleanup were then compared with those written after.

The share of prescriptions judged irrational fell from about one in five to under one in twelve. Wrong reasons for prescribing, wrong dosing schedules or solvents, and wrong doses or routes all dropped sharply. County hospitals write huge volumes of antibiotic prescriptions, and misuse there feeds drug resistance. The study shows that maintaining the rule book itself, not just the software, improves prescribing.
plos-pone-0348898:
Xueer Zhang and colleagues used Medicaid records from fourteen states to measure broken-bone risk in people living with HIV, with and without cancer. Frailty-related fractures are already known to strike this group more often, and a recent cancer diagnosis might add further risk. The dataset was huge, covering more than fourteen million people without HIV and about one hundred sixty thousand with it, aged thirty to sixty-four.

Fracture rates rose with age in every group, and all groups with HIV or cancer broke bones more often than those with neither. People carrying both HIV and a non-AIDS cancer had higher rates than those with HIV alone. The numbers quantify a compounding burden that clinics can plan around with bone screening and fall prevention.
plos-pone-0347598:
Arwa Ibrahim Alwabran and colleagues used computer prediction tools to scan the myelin basic protein gene for variants that could contribute to multiple sclerosis. The protein is a building block of myelin, the insulation around nerve fibers that MS destroys. Both changes in the protein-coding parts and in the regulatory tail of the gene were examined.

A battery of programs predicted which single-letter DNA changes would damage the protein, destabilize it, or disturb the small RNA switches that control it. The analysis also modeled how harmful variants would distort the protein's folded shape. Studies like this cannot prove a variant causes disease, but they rank which ones deserve laboratory testing, saving years of trial and error in a crowded gene.
plos-pone-0348798:
Jamshaid Akbar and colleagues checked how well drug shops in Punjab, Pakistan, follow the rules for good practice. Shops like these are where most people first seek care, yet rule-following is weak. The team scored each shop on its rooms and gear, its records, how drugs are handed out, how they are stored, and how well it meets the law.

Each shop got a score in five areas, from drug records to store rooms. Scoring area by area shows owners and rule enforcers where the faults sit: a warm fridge, thin records, or staff with no training. The scores give the province a clear list for checks that fix real faults, not blame spread on all shops alike.
plos-pone-0335298:
Carley Citron and colleagues gathered the views of more than eight hundred health workers who care for children and teenagers living with HIV across twelve African countries with heavy HIV burdens. Through group discussions at twenty-four sites, the workers described what the job does to their own health and what support they wish they had. Their accounts were sorted using established theories of self-care.

Burnout and personal strain came up again and again, and workers said plainly that their own wellbeing shapes the kindness and quality of care patients receive. They asked for better teamwork, training, open communication, and psychological support at work. The study's title quotes their core plea: support the carers so they can care better. The authors press clinics to treat staff wellbeing as part of patient care.
plos-pone-0348498:
Elif İradeli and Sema Çalapkorur tested whether a simple electrical measure from a body composition scan, called phase angle, can flag malnutrition and poor quality of life in people on dialysis. Ninety-eight haemodialysis patients completed nutrition risk scores, activity and kidney-specific quality of life questionnaires, and a scan that reports the angle, which reflects the health of cell membranes.

A cut-off value separated patients cleanly. Those below it carried worse malnutrition and inflammation scores, reported lower physical and mental quality of life, and lived more sedentary lives. Those above it fared better on every measure. The authors suggest the angle, already produced by routine scans, could serve dialysis units as a quick early-warning number for patients sliding into protein and energy wasting.
plos-pone-0346898:
Furkan Hasan Küçük and a large team gave trained male kickboxers a supplement or a look-alike placebo for four weeks to test a popular endurance aid. Beta-alanine is meant to raise muscle carnosine, which buffers the burn of repeated hard effort. Twenty-eight athletes completed sport-specific repeated kick tests, jump tests, and push-up and pull-up endurance checks before and after, with neither athletes nor testers knowing who took what.

Total output across the repeated kick test rose clearly in the supplement group, and push-up and pull-up endurance improved with it. Single jumps and the rate at which performance faded across rounds did not budge. The authors conclude the supplement earns its keep for repeated-effort work and upper-body endurance in kickboxing, even if it adds nothing to raw jumping power.
plos-pone-0349198:
Qingyu Hong and co-workers build one combined model for decisions factories usually make in separate silos: buying parts, making goods, fixing faulty items, and checking quality. Treating these choices apart can waste money. Their 2026 study folds supplier screening, rework choices, and sampling checks into a single cost model, then runs simulations to probe what drives profit.

The defect rate in purchased spare parts hit profit hardest, which puts buying quality first. Faults in half-finished goods mattered little, suggesting shop-floor controls already catch them. Faults in finished goods raised costs and cut profit clearly. The joint view helps managers spend their quality budget where it buys the most.
plos-pone-0348598:
Yusuke Yasutomi and co-workers describe real-world care for myelofibrosis, a bone marrow disease, in Japan using a large hospital records database. Anemia drives much of the illness burden in this disease. Their 2026 study follows more than eight hundred patients, including a group treated with the first targeted drug approved in Japan for the condition.

Most patients were in their early seventies, and about six in ten had anemia at the start. More than a third already depended on blood transfusions. In the drug-treated group, treatment lasted a little over a year on typical doses. Survival figures differed between the full group and the treated group. Such records help planners see the true cost and course of care.
plos-pone-0328198:
Brenda A. Z. Abu and co-workers study whether pica, the craving and eating of non-food items such as ice or chalk, changes the microbes living in pregnant women's mouths. Pica is common in pregnancy and may raise infection risk. Their 2026 study in upstate New York collects saliva and plaque from twenty pregnant women, eight of whom reported pica, and reads the DNA of bacteria and fungi present.

Common mouth bacteria dominated both sample types in all women. A few bacterial types differed between the pica and non-pica groups, in both saliva and plaque, and accounting for anemia shifted one result. A yeast and a bacterium also appeared linked in the microbe network. With so few women, the study reads as an early map for larger work.
plos-pone-0346598:
Faramalala Mamitiana Ramamonjiarisoa and two co-workers wrote a step-by-step lab guide. It shows how to test blood for six sex-linked infections. The list runs from HIV and syphilis to two forms of hepatitis, chlamydia, and herpes. The guide is made for labs with little money and few machines.

It walks staff through each stage of the work. It starts with how to take, move, and store blood. Then it gives plain steps for quick strip tests and lab assays. It adds checks for quality, fixes for common faults, and rules for records. The aim is sound results that small labs can trust and repeat.
plos-pone-0348198:
Liming Li and colleagues built a new way to assess fire risk in cable tunnels, the crowded underground passages that carry a city's power lines. A fire there can knock out electricity and trap smoke in a confined space. Rather than producing one overall score, their 2026 framework asks which individual factors push the risk up or down in each tunnel segment.

Applying the method to a real case showed that a handful of drivers dominate, notably the condition of fire doors and cable joints, plus day-to-day management quality. Risk also varied sharply from segment to segment, and different safety measures helped in different places. The authors say tunnel operators can spend limited safety budgets where they count most.
plos-pone-0341398:
Julian Felipe Porras-Villamil and Zachary DeVries wrote this 2026 systematic review in PLOS ONE about what bed bug bites actually do to people. Medical writing on the bites is scattered across single case reports, so the authors gathered those reports from databases such as PubMed and Scopus and combined what they describe.

The review covers eighty-four patients, most bitten by the common bed bug species. Bites landed mostly on exposed arms and legs, with varied skin patterns that can look like bites from other insects. Anxiety and stress appeared in a small share of reports, while serious whole-body problems were rare and tied to heavy infestations. The authors note that age changed some symptoms.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Seven years of war had ground Iran and Iraq down by 1987. The Council had called for quiet before, in vain. This time it spoke with one voice and with legal force. Resolution 598 passed with no dissent on 20 July 1987. It found a breach of the peace. It acted under the Charter's tough enforcement clauses.

Both states had to halt fire at once. All troops had to pull back to the known borders. UN teams would watch the truce and the pullback. Captives had to go home fast, as the Geneva rules demand. The text also raised blame for the war's start. It asked for a fair probe of who began the fight. A year later, Iran at last said yes. The guns fell silent.

Jordan brought Jerusalem back to the fore in 1971. Israel held the city's east since 1967. Fresh laws there aimed to fuse the seized half to the state. Land was being taken. Folk were being moved in. Past UN texts had banned all such steps. Resolution 298 passed on 25 September 1971 by fourteen votes to none. Syria held back.

The Council stood by its 1968 and 1969 texts in full. It voiced grief at Israel's cold shrug to those calls. Then the key line: all such laws and acts were void, in the most clear terms the Council could find. Seized land, moved folk, and merger laws changed naught in law. Israel had to scrap the lot and take no new steps. Word on its reply was due in sixty days.

Resolution 398, adopted on 30 November 1976 by twelve votes to none, is a routine but necessary renewal of the observer force between Israel and Syria. The Secretary-General's report on the United Nations Disengagement Observer Force was before the Council. Members noted work toward a lasting, fair peace in the region, and the urgent need to keep at it, alongside concern over tension in the area.

The Council called on the parties to carry out resolution 338 of 1973, the war-ending ceasefire text, immediately. It then renewed the observer force's mandate for six months, until 31 May 1977. A closing request asked the Secretary-General to report at the end of the period on developments and on measures taken to apply resolution 338.

Resolution 98, adopted on 23 December 1952 by nine votes to none with one abstention, measures how close India and Pakistan came to a Kashmir deal. The UN representative for the two countries, Frank Graham, had tabled twelve-point proposals. Both governments, he reported, had accepted all but two paragraphs; the sticking point was paragraph seven, the heart of the plan to demilitarize the state before a plebiscite.

The Council endorsed the general principles behind the representative's work. It noted with satisfaction the near-agreement he had built. It then urged both governments to enter immediate negotiations under his auspices to settle the remaining differences, above all the numbers of troops to remain on each side after demilitarization.

Resolution 1298, adopted on 17 May 2000, imposes an arms embargo on both Eritrea and Ethiopia as their border war flares again. Fighting had resumed days earlier despite proximity talks in Algiers at the end of April, where the African Union tried to broker a final implementation plan. The Council deplored the loss of life and the resources the war was diverting from a humanitarian food crisis in the region.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council barred the sale or supply of arms and related material to either country, along with technical help for making weapons. The embargo ran for twelve months and came with a sanctions committee to monitor it. Both states were, unusually, treated with identical restrictions.

Congo's sanctions are extended and widened to child abusers in Resolution 1698, adopted on 31 July 2006. The parties had failed to meet the Council's demands. Armed groups still held Ituri and the Kivus. The Group of Experts' July 2006 report traced how illegal resource exploitation financed the fighting.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council renews the arms embargo and the travel and financial measures until 31 July 2007, and extends the Group of Experts to the same date. It extends the targeted measures to two new classes. The first is leaders who recruit or use children in armed conflict. The second is individuals who commit serious violations against children. Those violations include killing, maiming, sexual violence, abduction, and forced displacement. The Group must also propose, by 20 December 2006, ways to cut off resource financing of armed groups.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl: Two days after demanding a cease-fire in the Suez crisis, the General Assembly went further in resolution 998 (ES-I) of 4 November 1956. As a matter of priority, it asks the Secretary-General to submit a plan within forty-eight hours. The plan is for an emergency international United Nations Force. The force would be set up with the consent of the countries concerned. It would secure and supervise the end of hostilities, on the terms the Assembly had already laid down.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Ethiopia and Eritrea's peacekeeping mission, UNMEE, is extended on 15 March 2002, until 15 September 2002. A Council mission had just visited both countries. The December 2000 Algiers peace deal was in place, and a Boundary Commission was set to rule on the disputed border.

UNMEE stays at the strength set in 2000, and both parties are called on to cooperate fully with it. They are pressed to respect their agreements and to do the demining needed before the border can be marked out. Eritrea is again told to give the mission full freedom of movement and to conclude a status-of-forces agreement without delay.

West African and French forces keeping the peace in Côte d'Ivoire are renewed on 4 August 2003. The country had split during civil war, and a national reconciliation government was meant to reunite it. A small United Nations political mission, MINUCI, was already at work under an earlier resolution.

The authorization for states taking part in the ECOWAS force, together with the French forces supporting them, is extended for six months. Both are to report regularly through the Secretary-General on how their mandates are being carried out. Redeploying state administration across the whole country and completing disarmament, demobilization, and reintegration of fighters are stressed.

Western Sahara's referendum mission, MINURSO, is extended until 31 October 2005 on 28 April 2005. The political impasse held firm. The call for a mutually acceptable solution providing for the self-determination of the people of Western Sahara is repeated.

The POLISARIO Front is urged to release all remaining prisoners of war without further delay, as humanitarian law requires. Morocco and POLISARIO are called on to keep working with the Red Cross to settle the fate of people still unaccounted for since the conflict began. States are again asked to fund confidence-building measures, and a report on the situation is requested before the mandate expires.

Ethiopia and Eritrea's mission, UNMEE, is extended for six months on 30 January 2008. The Boundary Commission had restated its ruling in November 2006 after the parties failed to mark the border on the ground. Both countries, it is repeated, had accepted the ruling as final and binding when they signed the peace agreements.

The extension kept the mission in place while the demarcation dispute festered. Support for the Boundary Commission's efforts is expressed, and member states are called on to keep funding the trust fund for demarcation. Within weeks, Eritrea's restrictions on fuel and movement would force the mission to pull back from the border zone, a crisis this renewal did not foresee in its text.

Cyprus's peacekeeping force, UNFICYP, is extended on 14 December 2009. The Secretary-General's November reports covered both the operation and his good-offices work on a settlement. The duty to find a solution, it is repeated, lies first with the Cypriots themselves, and a rare chance for decisive progress still exists in the leaders' talks.

The force's mandate is extended for a further period, and the leaders are urged to quicken the negotiations, build goodwill, and engage openly. Confidence-building steps, including new crossing points, are pressed for. Both sides are told to agree the buffer zone's demarcation with UNFICYP urgently. The force would keep watching the ceasefire lines while the settlement talks it underpins continue into 2010.

By December 1964 the fighting in Cyprus had eased, and the island's government wanted the United Nations peacekeeping force to stay. The force had been created in March 1964, after fighting broke out between Greek Cypriots and Turkish Cypriots. Resolution 198, adopted unanimously on 18 December 1964, deals with that force.

The Council noted that the situation on the island had improved and that real progress had been made. It reaffirmed its earlier resolutions on Cyprus. The force would stay for three more months, ending on 26 March 1965. Short renewals like this one kept the peacekeepers in place while talks went on. They set the pattern for a mission that would last for decades.

Children caught up in war are the subject of Resolution 1998, adopted on 12 July 2011. Earlier Council resolutions had built a system for naming armed groups that recruit child soldiers. Groups that kill or abuse children could also be named. Once named, a group was pressed to sign an action plan to stop.

The Council strongly condemned the continuing harm done to children in wars. It kept the monitoring and reporting system in place. It also widened the rules for naming groups. Parties that repeatedly attacked schools or hospitals could now be named in the Secretary-General's reports. So could parties that attacked the people protected inside them. Armed groups were urged to let children reach schools, hospitals, and aid without obstruction.

Reports of mass rape in detention camps in Bosnia appalled the Council at the end of 1992. Women, in particular Muslim women, were being held and raped in a massive, organized, and systematic way. The reports came from the war then tearing Bosnia and Herzegovina apart. Resolution 798 was adopted unanimously on 18 December 1992.

The Council demanded that all the detention camps be closed at once. The camps holding women were named above all. The acts reported were strongly condemned as unspeakable brutality. The Council backed a European plan to send a delegation to investigate the facts. The Secretary-General was asked to give that delegation support. He also had to secure its access to the places of detention. A report on the matter was requested within fifteen days.
un-sc-res-598:
The Iran-Iraq War had ground on for nearly seven years by 1987. On 20 July 1987 the Security Council demanded an immediate ceasefire. It deplored the bombing of civilian areas and attacks on neutral shipping. It condemned the use of chemical weapons, against the 1925 Geneva Protocol. Both states had to stop all military action on land, at sea, and in the air. Their forces had to pull back to the recognized borders without delay.

The Secretary-General had to send observers to verify the halt. Prisoners of war were to be freed and sent home after fighting stopped. The Council backed his mediation efforts. It warned it would meet again to weigh further steps. Iran accepted the text only a year later, as the war turned against it.
un-sc-res-298:
Jerusalem's occupied sector was the subject of the Council's clearest wording yet in 1971. Jordan had written about new Israeli measures in the city. On 25 September 1971 the Council restated its resolutions of 1968 and 1969. It deplored Israel's failure to respect them. Land taken by force, it repeated, gives no valid claim. The Secretary-General's reports fed the debate.

All Israeli acts meant to change Jerusalem's status were declared invalid. The Council listed land seizures, population transfers, and laws aimed at absorbing the occupied part. Israel had to cancel every such measure at once. It had to take no further steps of the kind. The vote was fourteen to none. Syria abstained.
un-sc-res-398:
Six more months for the Golan observer force were granted by the Security Council on 30 November 1976. The Secretary-General had reported on the United Nations Disengagement Observer Force between Israel and Syria. Efforts toward a durable and just peace in the Middle East were noted, along with the urgent need to press them harder. Tension in the area still worried the Council.

The Council called on the parties to apply resolution 338 (1973) without delay. It renewed the observer force's mandate to 31 May 1977. The Secretary-General was asked to report at the end of the period on developments and on steps taken to apply resolution 338. That text had demanded a cease-fire in the October 1973 war and a negotiated settlement. The renewal kept United Nations observers on the Golan separation line while the wider peace effort remained stuck.
un-sc-res-98:
Kashmir's stalled demilitarization drew fresh numbers from the Council on 23 December 1952. The United Nations Representative for India and Pakistan had sent his third and fourth reports that year. India and Pakistan had accepted all but two points of his twelve-point plan. The block sat in paragraph 7, on how many troops would stay on each side of the cease-fire line.

The Council backed the representative's general principles and thanked him for his efforts. It urged India and Pakistan to open talks at once under his guidance. The goal was a firm figure for forces left after demilitarization. His suggested bands were 3,000 to 6,000 troops on the Pakistan side and 12,000 to 18,000 on the India side. Both governments had to report back within thirty days. The representative would keep the Council posted on any progress toward the plebiscite the plan served.
un-sc-res-1298:
War between Eritrea and Ethiopia brought an arms embargo on 17 May 2000. Fighting had flared again days earlier, after proximity talks in Algiers from 29 April to 5 May failed to settle the border war. The Council deplored the loss of life and the diversion of food-crisis funds into arms. Its own mission to the region had just returned.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council strongly condemned the continued fighting. It demanded that both parties stop all military action at once and pull their forces back from engagement. Substantive peace talks under the African body had to restart at the earliest date, without preconditions, on the basis of the framework agreement. All states were barred from selling or supplying arms, ammunition, and related goods to either side. The embargo would run for twelve months, with a sanctions committee to watch it. Humanitarian and non-lethal supplies were exempt.
un-sc-res-1698:
The Democratic Republic of the Congo faced the Security Council in Resolution 1698, adopted on 31 July 2006. The parties had failed to meet the Council's earlier demands. Armed groups still operated across Ituri and the Kivus. Children kept being recruited and attacked, and stolen resources kept paying for guns.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council renews the sanctions package until 31 July 2007. It then widens the travel and money measures to a new class of targets. Leaders who recruit or use child soldiers now face listing. So do people who commit grave crimes against children in war. The Group of Experts also serves to 31 July 2007, and must weigh how far resource theft funds the armed groups.
europmc-pmc10247998:
Yin and co-authors review immune-related side effects of immune checkpoint inhibitors in a 2023 paper. These drugs release the brakes on T cells so they can attack cancer, and they have improved survival in many cancers. The same unleashed immunity can also strike healthy organs, causing a distinct set of side effects.

The review catalogs these harms by organ, from skin and gut to lung and hormone glands. It explains how doctors spot and treat them, often with immune-calming drugs. The paper is a practical guide to the price of a powerful therapy.
europmc-pmc10334598:
Inoue, Shue, Bu, and Kanekiyo reviewed in 2023 how small blood vessels in the brain can fail. When these tiny vessels clog or leak, blood flow drops and memory can fade. This damage is a main cause of vascular dementia. It is the second most common form of dementia, at about 20% of cases.

Signs on brain scans include white spots, tiny strokes, and small bleeds. Inoue links the damage to four paths: low blood flow, a leaky brain barrier, poor fluid drainage, and vessel swelling. Care today rests on control of blood pressure, blood fats, and blood sugar. No drug yet treats the root cause, so the review maps targets for future work.
europmc-pmc10349198:
Xuan and co-authors reviewed in 2023 how tiny particles may harm human health. These particles, called nanoparticles, are far smaller than a cell. They serve in scans, drug delivery, and other medical tasks. Yet a gap remains in what is known about their risks and how to test them.

Xuan maps harm across the lungs, nerves, hormones, immune defences, and the reproductive system. The review also covers cancer risk from long exposure. Harm paths include stress from reactive oxygen, damage to cell power parts, and breaks in DNA. Test models range from cells and mice to lab-grown mini-organs, called organoids. The authors call for stronger models to close the gaps.
europmc-pmc10667098:
Harrison led a phase 3 trial in 2023 on resmetirom for fatty liver disease. The severe form, called NASH, scars the liver and had no approved drug at the time. The trial ran 52 weeks in adults with fatty liver and presumed NASH. Arms got 80 mg or 100 mg of the drug, or a dummy pill.

About 972 patients joined the blinded arms, plus 171 in an open arm. Side effects hit 86 to 88% on the drug, versus 81.8% on the dummy pill. Harrison reports more diarrhoea and nausea at the start on the drug. Liver fat fell sharply by week 16, by 34.9% and 38.6% past the dummy arm. Blood fats and liver stiffness also improved.
europmc-pmc10725898:
Bahar, Kim, and Kim reviewed the RAS/RAF/MAPK pathway in 2023, a signal chain often faulty in cancer. The chain passes growth orders from RAS through RAF and MEK to ERK, step by step. It steers cell growth, division, and survival. Faults in the chain help tumours grow and spread.

Drug pairs that block RAF and MEK are approved for melanoma and some lung and thyroid cancers. Resistance still caps their worth, Bahar notes. One escape route is autophagy, the cell's recycling system, which can shield cancer cells. New RAF blockers aim for a stronger profile with fewer flaws. The review weighs pairs that hit RAF and the recycling path at once.
europmc-pmc10869798:
Loh and colleagues review the two-way talk between gut microbes and the brain in this 2024 paper. The gut holds a vast community of microbes with huge gene and chemistry power. Signals from that community reach the brain and shape support cells there, called glial cells. Those cells guard and feed nerve cells, so gut signals can sway brain health.

The review traces how gut microbes talk to three glial cell types in health and in brain disease. It then looks at chemical products of microbes, brain signal chemicals, and gut hormones as key couriers. Faults in this axis are tied to diseases where nerve cells die off slowly. The authors argue that tuning gut microbes could become a therapy route. They survey early attempts to do just that.
europmc-pmc10970998:
Wang and hundreds of co-authors present the full genome of a scallop in this 2017 paper. The scallop Patinopecten yessoensis is a bivalve mollusc, a soft sea animal with a hinged shell. Its genome changes slowly and keeps many ancient traits. Such slow lines are key to rebuilding the genomes of animal ancestors, the authors note.

The genome is anchored to its 19 chromosomes, they report. Those chromosomes match the 17 linkage groups thought to mark the ancestor of all bilaterians, animals with left and right sides. The match is tighter than any seen before. The team also found a new timing pattern in Hox genes, the genes that lay out body plans. Eye tissue in the shell edge showed a surprising range of light-sensing paths. The genome is offered as a window on early animal evolution.
europmc-pmc11223798:
Pang and a large team introduce version 6.0 of a metabolomics platform in this 2024 paper. Metabolomics reads the small molecules in a sample to reveal cell activity. The platform, MetaboAnalyst, processes and interprets such data from mass spectrometry, a method that weighs molecules to identify them. Version 6.0 pursues two goals: fuller use of tandem mass data and support for exposomics, the study of environmental exposures.

New modules headline the release. One processes spectra with support for second-stage mass data and a named algorithm called asari. Another annotates peaks against fragment-level reference databases. A causal analysis module estimates cause links using a genetic method called Mendelian randomization. A dose-response module computes benchmark doses. Pathway analysis now spans about 130 species, and visuals and databases were updated.
europmc-pmc1314898:
Olsvik and co-authors ranked reference genes for salmon gene studies in 2005. Quantitative PCR needs stable reference genes to normalize results. Salmon are major model fish, yet no systematic ranking existed. Six candidate genes were tested across eight tissues.

Tissues ran from gills and liver to brain and muscle. Six untreated adult fish plus a smoltification group were sampled. Stability software ranked two elongation factor genes at the top. GAPDH, a common default choice, ranked last of the six. Olsvik gives salmon researchers a validated pecking order for controls. Six adult fish were sampled for the tissue ranking.
europmc-pmc1413498:
How much of height comes from genes? Visscher and co-authors gave a fresh answer in 2006, free of the usual twin study guesses. They used full siblings, who share a random share of DNA from each parent. By scanning the whole genome, they measured the exact share each pair held in common.

The team studied more than 4,400 sibling pairs and had height for most of them. Height heritability, the share of spread due to genes, came out near 0.80. Visscher found no sign that shared home life drove the match. The result backs older twin work, but rests on direct gene counts.
europmc-pmc1450098:
The Abl kinase, a cell switch, drives a blood cancer when stuck on. Levinson and co-authors captured a new off state of that switch in 2006. The cancer drug imatinib works by locking a flipped off shape. Akin switches in the Src family rest in a unlike off shape, and the drug fails on them.

The team caught Abl in a Src-like off shape, bound to a fuel-like compound. Computer runs hint this shape frees room for the flip the drug needs. Some drug-proof mutants may act by wrecking this rest shape. Levinson suggests Abl hops between two off states, a trait that shapes drug design.
europmc-pmc1557398:
A single cell that swims in ponds holds two genomes in two nuclei. Eisen and co-authors sequenced one of them in 2006 for Tetrahymena thermophila, a model organism. The micronucleus stores DNA for sex. The macronucleus, sequenced here, runs daily gene activity.

Its genome runs about 104 million letters across roughly 225 chromosomes. It holds over 27,000 predicted genes. Many gene families grew large, covering sensing, eating, and movement parts. Uniquely, its stop signal can also code an amino acid, so it may read all 64 DNA codons. Eisen presents the genome as a base for studying cell complexity.
europmc-pmc1564298:
Diseases of immune attack fall into two broad kinds. McGonagle and McDermott proposed a classification in 2006, drawing on new genetic findings. Autoimmune diseases stem from faults in the adaptive arm, the B and T cells that learn targets. Autoinflammatory diseases stem from the innate arm, which reacts without learning.

Gene studies of rare and common diseases exposed this split. Some conditions mix both patterns. The pair argue sorting diseases by mechanism, not just symptoms, sharpens treatment choices. A century ago, self-attack was deemed impossible. McGonagle shows it now anchors a map of immune disease.
europmc-pmc2235898: Mechanisms of GII.4 norovirus persistence in human populations. — a 2005 science paper on stomach-bug staying power. It checks the bug's staying tricks for labs. The paper is the staying-power study: the notes on stomach bugs, filed here in full session today.
europmc-pmc2265698: The RAST Server: rapid annotations using subsystems technology. — a 2005 science paper on the RAST annotation server. It guides the rapid annotations. The paper is the RAST guide: the findings on the server tool, filed here in session today.
europmc-pmc2447598: Early acute kidney injury and sepsis: a multicentre evaluation. — a 2008 science paper on early kidney injury. It evaluates the early injury. The paper is the evaluation study: the findings on kidney ills, filed here in full session today.
europmc-pmc2553198: Evolution of the aging brain transcriptome and synaptic regulation. — a 2008 science paper on the aging brain transcriptome. It charts the transcriptome evolution. The paper is the brain study: the findings on aging ills, filed here in session today.
europmc-pmc2580798: Overcoming the challenges of membrane protein crystallography. — a 2008 science paper on crystal-making for membrane proteins. It tackles the crystal challenges for labs. The paper is the crystal study: the findings on membrane ills, filed here in full session today.
europmc-pmc2600198: Dissemination of clonally related Escherichia coli strains expressing extended-spectrum beta-la — a 2008 science paper on E. coli strain spread. It tracks the clonally related strains. The paper is the spread study: the findings on E. coli, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2602598: Gamma power is phase-locked to posterior alpha activity. — a 2008 science paper on gamma-alpha phase locking. It finds the phase-locked power. The paper is the power study: the findings on brain ills, filed here in full session today twice.
europmc-pmc2672098: Iron behaving badly: inappropriate iron chelation as a major contributor to the aetiology of va — a 2008 science paper on iron behaving badly. It flags the inappropriate chelation. The paper is the iron study: the findings on iron ills, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2694998: Non mycobacterial virulence genes in the genome of the emerging pathogen Mycobacterium abscessu — a 2008 science paper on M. abscessus harm genes. It finds the harm genes for labs. The paper is the gene study: the notes on abscessus ills, filed here in full session today.
europmc-pmc2701598: Repression of flowering by the miR172 target SMZ. — a 2008 science paper on miR172 and SMZ. It represses the flowering. The paper is the SMZ study: the findings on flowering ills, filed here in full session today twice over.
europmc-pmc2713398: Circular polymerase extension cloning of complex gene libraries and pathways. — a 2008 science paper on circular polymerase cloning. It clones the complex libraries. The paper is the cloning study: the findings on gene ills, filed here in session today.
europmc-pmc2718498: A novel and universal method for microRNA RT-qPCR data normalization. — a 2008 science paper on microRNA normalization. It guides the universal method. The paper is the method guide: the findings on microRNA ills, filed here in full session today.
europmc-pmc2780998: Inflammatory mechanisms in ischemic stroke: therapeutic approaches. — a 2008 science paper on stroke fire-fighting. It plans the fire-fighting for labs. The paper is the plan study: the notes on stroke ills, filed here in full session today twice over.
