europmc-pmc2781298: Comprehensive functional analysis of Mycobacterium tuberculosis toxin-antitoxin systems: implic — a 2008 science paper on TB toxin-antitoxin. It analyzes the comprehensive systems. The paper is the system study: the findings on TB ills, filed here in full session today twice.
europmc-pmc2790698: Risk factors for delayed presentation and referral of symptomatic cancer: evidence for common c — a 2008 science paper on delayed cancer presentation. It lists the delayed risk factors. The paper is the factor study: the findings on cancer ills, filed here in session.
blau-altjudische-zauberwesen-1898:
Ludwig Blau published the first systematic survey of ancient Jewish magic in 1898, in German. His study drew on rabbinic literature, inscriptions, and archaeological finds. Amulets, angel names, and exorcisms all fall within his map.

Blau showed that magic ran alongside official religion, not apart from it. Rabbis condemned some practices while quietly accepting others in daily life. Folk cures, demon beliefs, and protective charms receive orderly treatment. The book was written for scholars and remains the subject's starting point. Later work on the Talmud and magic bowls builds on Blau's frame. His German title translates as the ancient Jewish magic system.
testament-of-solomon-conybeare-1898:
F. C. Conybeare translated the Testament of Solomon into English in 1898. His version appeared in the Jewish Quarterly Review that year. In the text, King Solomon interrogates demons one by one.

Each spirit must give its name, its mischief, and the angel who thwarts it. Solomon then sets the demons to work building the Temple. The dialogue mixes demonology with adventure and practical spell lore. Conybeare introduced Western readers to the fountainhead of Solomonic grimoire literature. Later grimoires borrowed its demon lists and angelic seals for centuries. The translation opened a strange, influential text to English scholarship.
high-history-holy-graal-evans-1898:
The High History of the Holy Graal is Sebastian Evans's 1898 English version of the French romance called Perlesvaus. Its author is unknown. The French original is among the strangest of all Grail books, and Evans kept its wildness intact.

Gawain and Perceval ride out on quests that fill thirty-five branches, or chapters, of the tale. They meet violence, visions, and marvels that test faith as much as courage. Castles, hermits, and strange beasts crowd the road. Readers who know only Malory's Grail will find this one fiercer and more fevered, closer to a dream than to a chronicle.
gawain-green-knight-weston-1898:
Sir Gawain and the Green Knight is a Middle English poem by an unknown fourteenth-century author. Jessie Weston retold it in plain English prose in 1898. Her version opened the poem to readers who could not face the old language.

A giant green knight rides into Camelot at Christmas and offers a game. Any man may strike him once with an axe, if Gawain will take the same blow in a year. Gawain accepts, cuts off the stranger's head, and watches him pick it up and ride away. What follows tests Gawain's courage, honesty, and honor at the Green Chapel.
molitor-de-lamiis-latin-1498:
Ulrich Molitor, a lawyer at Constance, wrote his dialogue on witches and pythonesses in the fifteenth century. This edition of 1498 is the first printed demonology with woodcuts, and the pictures are part of its fame. Molitor stages a debate over how much power the devil truly has over witches.

His speakers weigh famous cases and test the claims made for flight, storms, and transformations. Molitor grants the devil much, yet doubts the witches' own powers. The woodcuts show witches at their cauldron in early printed form. Quaint and grim by turns, the book set the new craft of print to serve the old fear. A later reprint also rides inside the library's 1580 Malleus volume.
plos-pone-0004898:
Rita Willemssen, Thomas Müller, and Michael Schwarz studied response monitoring in de novo patients with Parkinson disease, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Parkinson disease is accompanied by dysfunctions in cognitive processes including error processing, which depends on phasic decreases of medial prefrontal dopaminergic activity. No study had evaluated these processes in newly diagnosed, untreated patients, prompting electrophysiological assessment before medication confounds brain responses.

Early error monitoring is already altered at diagnosis. Cognitive changes begin alongside motor symptoms. Baseline measures enable treatment monitoring. De novo cohorts are scientifically precious. The results give future studies a clearer base for comparison and follow up. The team also set out clear next steps for work in this field. More tests with more samples will help show how strong the effect is. Such work helps guide care, field work, and lab work in the years ahead.
plos-pone-0004998:
Medulloblastoma is a childhood brain tumor. Rare cancer stem cells help drive it and resist treatment. Livia Garzia and colleagues studied a tiny RNA in these tumors. Their PLOS ONE paper appeared in 2009. The RNA is microRNA-199b-5p. MicroRNAs control genes by negative regulation.

They found this microRNA impairs the cancer stem cells. It works by holding down a gene called HES1. Restoring the microRNA weakened the tumor's stem cell core. The work spotlights a small molecule with large potential. It suggests a new angle against a deadly childhood cancer. Treatments that restore lost microRNAs could complement existing therapy.
plos-pone-0005098:
Gene activity over time is noisy and hard to read. Jianfeng Feng and colleagues borrowed a tool from audio engineering. Their PLOS ONE paper appeared in 2009. They analyzed microarray data in the frequency domain. Sound engineers break signals into pitches that way. Gene rhythms can be broken down similarly.

Their approach includes normalization, clustering and network analysis. An error model first cleans the data. The frequency view then reveals rhythms hidden in time. Patterns emerge that time plots obscure. The method gives biologists a new ear for gene data. It suits studies of cycles, like cell division and daily rhythms. Listening to genes turns a metaphor into a working method.
plos-pone-0005198:
Neisseria meningitidis, the germ behind meningitis, must have iron to live. Inside the human host, iron comes bound to different proteins in the throat and in the blood. Jordan and Saunders argued in PLOS ONE in 2009 that those proteins also tell the germ where it is.

When iron is scarce, the bacterium changes which genes it uses so it can grab and spare iron. The mix of iron-binding proteins around it differs by body site, forming a niche signal. Reading that signal may help the germ switch between quiet colonization and invasive disease.
plos-pone-0005298:
Stromatolites are layered rock structures that may hold Earth's earliest signs of life. Reading those signs is risky, since modern microbes can contaminate ancient samples. Gérard and colleagues drilled pristine stromatolite cores in Western Australia and reported their findings in PLOS ONE in 2009.

The fossil samples come from the Fortescue Group and are about 2.7 billion years old. Inside them, the team found modern subsurface bacteria. Their presence is a warning: life found in ancient rock may be a recent guest, and claims about early life must rule that out.
plos-pone-0005898:
Shreedhar Natarajan and Eric Jakobsson built a method in 2009 to match proteins with their true counterparts across species. Comparing genomes requires knowing which protein in one species does the same job as a protein in another. Simple similarity searches often pick the wrong match among look-alikes.

Their algorithm, MoLFunCs, finds the most likely functional counterpart using network ideas and trusted sources. Better matches mean better transfer of knowledge from model organisms to humans. Drug and disease research leans on such transfers daily. The paper offers a heuristic that weighs function over raw resemblance.
plos-pone-0005998:
Balancing a pole on a fingertip looks like play, yet it obeys strict math. Tyler Cluff and Ramesh Balasubramaniam tracked learners at that task in 2009. Six people practiced pole balancing over three sessions, sitting and standing, while their PLOS ONE study recorded the speed changes of the fingertip in a sideways plane.

The speed changes follow a heavy-tailed pattern called a Lévy distribution, and its slope fell as skill grew. A changing number thus marks the course of learning itself. The work gives motor learning a compact sign to follow, and it shows how a simple task can expose the deep rules by which people gain control of their own movement.
plos-pone-0006098:
Blood from a lupus patient is a blend, and the blend hides which cells are switched on. Alexander Abbas, Kristen Wolslegel, Dhaya Seshasayee and colleagues unmixed that blend on paper in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper deconvolves blood microarray data from systemic lupus erythematosus, an autoimmune disease with sweeping changes in white blood cell counts and activity.

Working backward from mixed data, the method recovers cellular activation patterns cell type by cell type. That recovery matters because lupus care lacks sharp markers for flares. A tool that reads the immune system's state from one blood sample could guide dosing and warn of worsening disease before symptoms declare it.
plos-pone-0006198:
Feeling sure about a judgment is usually tied to being right, but Eric Fimbel, Rene Michaud, and Mathieu Martin question that link. Their 2009 PLOS ONE study deals with judging sizes and sorting them into classes. From an observer's view, a person who answers the same way each time looks reliably certain.

The authors argue that certainty tracks the consistency of judgments more closely than their accuracy. A steady judge can be steadily wrong, yet still appear sure. That split matters wherever confidence is used as proof, from eyewitness accounts to expert panels. The paper offers a fresh way to test and measure self-confidence.
plos-pone-0006698:
Shobana Rebecca Dissanayeke and colleagues studied a gene variant and childhood tuberculosis in PLOS ONE in 2009. The gene is TIRAP, which helps pass signals from immune sensors. Those sensors, called toll-like receptors, recognize molecules on mycobacteria. Earlier work had linked TIRAP variants to resistance or risk for several infections. The authors asked whether the same holds for tuberculosis in children.

Their answer was mixed and depended on the group studied. Variation in TIRAP was not linked to general childhood tuberculosis risk. It may, however, affect risk of tuberculous meningitis in some ethnic groups. Meningitis is the most dangerous form of the disease in children. The findings argue for testing genetic risk separately across populations.
plos-pone-0006798:
Luu Thi Lien and colleagues measured tuberculosis infection among hospital workers in Hanoi in PLOS ONE in 2009. TB spreads to health care workers worldwide. Infection control should reduce spread inside hospitals. Yet worker infection is rarely measured in high-burden countries. Vietnam is one such country.

The team ran a cross-sectional study of hospital staff. They estimated prevalence of TB infection among the workers. They also identified risk factors linked to being infected. High infection rates would signal weak points in hospital control. The results give Vietnamese hospitals evidence for protecting their own staff.
plos-pone-0006898:
Zong-Ming Xie and colleagues moved two soybean genes into a model plant to test stress protection in PLOS ONE in 2009. The genes encode trihelix transcription factors, GmGT-2A and GmGT-2B. Trihelix factors guide light responses and development. Their role in abiotic stress was largely unclear. Abiotic stresses include drought, salt, and cold.

Transgenic Arabidopsis carrying the soybean genes tolerated stresses better. Improved tolerance shows the factors do act in stress defense. Soybean is a major world crop facing harsher climates. Genes that protect a model plant may protect crops too. The work nominates two candidates for stress-resistant breeding.
plos-pone-0006998:
Thomas Quack, Jürgen Knobloch, Svenja Beckmann, and colleagues studied parasite reproduction in PLOS ONE in 2009. Schistosomiasis is a major parasitic disease of humans and animals. The worm's eggs drive much of the illness. So the processes that build the worm's gonads are prime targets for intervention.

Working in Schistosoma mansoni, the team characterized a formin protein called SmDia. They showed it interacts with a Src kinase and a small GTPase in the gonads. Those partnerships suggest how egg production is organized. Blocking them might reduce the eggs that cause disease.
plos-pone-0007098:
Silke Schüle, Björn-Philipp Kloke, Julia Kaiser, and colleagues studied HIV's block in monocytes in PLOS ONE in 2009. Human monocytes resist infection by HIV-1. HIV-based gene delivery vectors also fail in them. Yet vectors from a simian virus, SIV of sooty mangabeys, enter monocytes in a single round with ease.

The team traced that difference to a viral protein called Vpx. The version from the strain SIVsmmPBj abolished the restriction. In plain terms, Vpx removes a guard that keeps HIV out. Knowing the guard's identity matters for both cure research and vector design.
plos-pone-0007198:
Martin Pyka, Christian F. Beckmann, Sonja Schöning, and colleagues reported a brain imaging study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Their subject is the default-mode network, a set of brain areas active at rest. This network quiets down during hard thinking tasks, and it matters for psychiatric research.

The authors ask whether a demanding working memory task changes later resting brain patterns. They use fMRI scans to compare rest periods that follow different levels of mental load. Their results show that effort can leave a trace in the brain even after the task ends.
plos-pone-0007298:
Caroline V. Palmer, Chintan K. Modi, and Laura D. Mydlarz tested a new role for glowing coral proteins in PLOS ONE in 2009. Anthozoans such as corals carry a wide array of fluorescent proteins. Their biochemical traits and function in host tissue remained to be determined when the study began.

Fluorescent proteins often increase in injured or compromised coral tissue. That pattern suggested a protective role. The authors test whether coral fluorescent proteins act as antioxidants, mopping up damaging oxygen molecules. A confirmed role would recast coral color as part of a stress defense system.
openalex-w2058652198: Yasuní may be Earth's most biodiverse patch — oil sits beneath it. Bass and colleagues' 2010 paper laid out the global conservation significance of Ecuador's Yasuní National Park. The work weighed the park's biodiversity against the ITT oil reserves below.
openalex-w2103160998: Amazon soils vary wildly — their birth explains why. A 2010 study measured chemical and physical traits of Amazon forest soils against their origins. The 71-plot survey across six countries mapped soil diversity for the RAINFOR project.
plos-pone-0006298:
Cells respond to broken DNA with a coordinated alarm and repair program. Maria Quanz and colleagues jammed that alarm in a 2009 PLOS ONE study using molecules that mimic double-strand breaks. The earliest steps of damage recognition in mammal cells are still not fully understood.

The fake breaks hyperactivated DNA-PK, a key damage-sensing enzyme, and disorganised the whole response. Flooding the sensor shows how its tuning shapes downstream choices. The experiment reveals wiring that normal damage levels hide. It may also suggest ways to sensitise cancer cells to DNA-breaking treatments.
plos-pone-0009698:
Celiac disease is best known for gut damage caused by an immune reaction to gluten. Sabrina Boscolo and colleagues tested whether its signature antibodies can also harm movement and balance. Their mouse study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010.

The antibodies target transglutaminase, an enzyme found in many tissues, including the brain. Mice given the antibodies developed ataxia, a shaky and unsteady way of moving. That result ties a celiac-linked immune response to damage in balance control. The finding came from direct tests in living mice. It offers a clue for patients whose celiac disease comes with nerve symptoms.
openalex-w2163192098: Some metals can be bent out of shape and then — with a little heat — snap back to their original form. This 2003 review surveys shape memory alloys and their "pseudoelastic" behavior for medicine: stents that expand inside arteries, orthodontic wires, and surgical tools that flex without breaking. The paper explains the physics behind the trick and where these smart materials are headed in the clinic.
openalex-w2918389998: Plant breeding runs on the breeder's equation — the math linking selection to genetic gain. This 2019 Theoretical and Applied Genetics paper distills lessons for public-sector breeding programs: how new technologies, aligned with quantitative and Mendelian genetics, can deliver step changes in productivity. The message is that better breeding is as much about method as about tools.
openalex-w3015355998: Feeding the world sustainably is the century's great food challenge — and innovation may be the fastest lever. This 2020 Nature Food paper, by Herrero, Thornton, Mason-D'Croz and colleagues, argues that innovation can accelerate the transition to a sustainable food system. The authors map where new technologies and practices could matter most.
europmc-pmc2842698: Where climates keep shifting, life never rests. This 2010 essay by Graham Bell probes ever-shifting natural picks as the engine that renews fitness in fickle settings. The author holds that swing keeps gene mix rich. The piece frames evolution in a restless world.
europmc-pmc2843598: Trading butter fats for seed fats is old diet lore, but does it spare hearts? This 2010 pool of top-trial proof says yes for heart disease. The authors fused trial sums on heart outcomes. The blend firmed the swap's case.
europmc-pmc2880998: Brain inflammation drives many ills, and this 2010 lab study tests a calming drug. The authors show dimethylfumarate cools microglial and astrocyte inflammation by cutting nitric oxide and key immune signals. Their dish work revealed the mechanism. The finding backed a drug later used in multiple sclerosis.
europmc-pmc2881098: France launched a giant online nutrition study, and this 2010 paper introduces it. The authors describe the Nutrinet-Santé Study, a web-based project linking diet to health in tens of thousands. Their design pioneered internet epidemiology. The study became a powerhouse of nutrition evidence.
europmc-pmc2882898: Staying active keeps elders able, and this 2010 review gathers the proof. The authors survey physical activity against functional limits in older adults, tied to Canada's activity guidelines. Their synthesis backs moving more at every age. The review underpins public advice for aging well and staying independent.
europmc-pmc3002198: Farm pesticides may dull young minds. This 2010 study links pesticide exposure to attention gaps in young Mexican-American farmworker kids. The authors' findings warn their families. Their work shaped safety rules. Mothers' urine samples told the exposure story. Buffer zones around fields grew after it.
europmc-pmc3031198: Comparing species' pasts needs clever math. This 2011 paper brings a tool that compares the histories of many species at once. The authors' method handles rate differences. Their tool spread through labs. Ice ages left shared marks it can read. The method runs on standard lab computers.
europmc-pmc3091298: Exome capture got automated. This 2011 paper automates building human exome libraries ready for sequencing. The authors' pipeline slashed costs. Their method powered genomics. Robots now prep thousands of exomes. Rare-disease labs adopted it at once. The pipeline runs with minimal hands.
europmc-pmc3116198: Crohn's gut damage got a score. This 2011 paper builds the Lémann score for Crohn's digestive damage. The authors turn scans into numbers. Their score guides treatment. Higher scores predicted surgery need. Doctors now track scores over years. The score standardizes clinical trials.
europmc-pmc3126798: Scientists' data-sharing habits got surveyed. This 2011 paper studies researchers' data sharing practices and perceptions. The authors reveal the barriers. Their work pushed open-data policies. Fear of scooping topped the excuses. Funders now mandate sharing plans. The survey is widely cited.
europmc-pmc3177898: Severe depression showed brain inflammation. This 2011 paper links severe depression to microglial quinolinic acid in the cingulate gyrus. The authors reveal the immune link. Their work points to new drugs. The acid overstimulates brain cells. Anti-inflammatory drugs are now in trials.
europmc-pmc3180398: Diabetes risk models got graded. This 2011 review assesses methods and reporting of type 2 diabetes prediction models. The authors find shaky quality. Their work tightened standards. Most models lacked validation, they found. New checklists now guide builders. The review shaped reporting rules.

20994-kilgorman-a-story-of-ireland-in-17:
Reed scorned tales that hid moral powder in jam, says the note that fronts Kilgorman. Such dosing, he held, spoils the jam and sickens the reader of the powder. Blood-and-thunder penny tales earn his scorn from the other flank as well.

Kilgorman tells of Ireland in 1798, the year of the great rising. Talbot Baines Reed sets a boy amid rebels, redcoats, and a land aflame. He aims for thrills with truth, not shocks for their own sake. The book shows a boys' writer at his most ambitious, facing a grim, real war with care and pace.
20393-a-short-history-of-english-printin:
Printing came to England in 1476, and this short history follows the craft through to 1898. It moves press by press and printer by printer. The writer based the account on personal study of the books and fragments each press produced.

For the earliest period, the book draws on detailed Sandars Lectures about the first printers' work. Originality, it notes, is out of the question for that age, so care and proof matter most. The history gives students of books a compact map of how English printing grew from Caxton's day to the modern trade.

Lorenzo Casalino and co-authors present Double Strike, an attack on side-channel defenses for neural networks. Their 2026 arXiv paper notes that deep networks support driving assistants and medical diagnoses. Training them is lengthy and expensive, so the trained weights are valuable intellectual property.

Side-channel analysis has emerged as an effective way to recover those weights from implementations. Defenses based on approximation aim to block such recovery. Double Strike shows how to break approximation-based countermeasures, per the title. For chip and model vendors, the result is a warning: defenses must be tested against adaptive attacks before deployed networks can be called protected.

The paper also gives a step-by-step way to build the bounds from data. This widens the class of systems that can pass a formal check. It is not just what can be run in a test on a screen. The work helps where safety must be proved, not just hoped for.
