The setting is a class of AdS3 solutions in type IIB supergravity that preserve a certain amount of supersymmetry. Equivariant localization is the method: symmetry can pin a hard integral down to a few special points. Couzens applies it to several observables of these solutions.

His route to localize the odd-dimensional internal space is unusual. He reduces along a shrinking circle, which creates a boundary in the remaining even-dimensional spacetime. That boundary makes the localization workable. Results like these feed the holographic dictionary linking gravity solutions to field theories. The paper is written for string theorists who compute exact quantities in supersymmetric backgrounds.
arxiv-2601-07998:
Hongwei Lin and colleagues predict where people will look in a visual search, using texture and oriented filter features. Understanding human visual search matters for vision science and computer vision. It also models how observers allocate attention when a target's location is unknown. Their 2026 preprint studies the link between Gabor features and texture features from gray-level co-occurrence matrices. The focus is early-stage search behavior.

Early attention decides which regions get examined at all. Statistical texture may tell the visual system where a target is plausible. Comparing two feature families shows which better tracks human gaze. Such models feed image quality assessment and interface design. The paper serves vision scientists and medical imaging scholars. It continues a line of work on predicting regions of interest in search tasks.
arxiv-2601-06898:
Sonia Yeh wrote a 2026 arXiv paper with Rishabh Ghotge, Yujia Shi, and Luka de Koe. The paper sets out a score for how well a truck charge site holds up under stress. The sites serve heavy-duty trucks and charge at megawatt scale. The score is called a Resilience Key Performance Indicator, or Resilience KPI.

The score does not rest on one kind of threat. It tracks how a site holds up when parts fail or load spikes. It uses signs that staff can see on site each day. These signs cover how long the site can ride through a fault. They cover how fast it can get back to full work. They cover work kept up with one part out of use. They also cover charge not served and lines of trucks that wait.
arxiv-2601-07198: Yan Xie and Junjie Liu wrote a 2026 arXiv paper on how to read the heat of a tiny quantum system. The field is quantum thermometry. It does for tiny systems what a home thermometer does at our scale. Heat is not a trait quantum rules let us read at once. Most past work set bounds on how sharp such a read can be, via the quantum Fisher information and the Cramer-Rao bound. Xie and Liu work on a system out of balance, with a direct readout as the aim.
arxiv-2601-08098: Philip Korman wrote a 2026 arXiv paper on a broad form of Pohozhaev's identity for radial solutions of p-Laplace equations. An identity of this kind gives a sum that each solution must match, which can rule out solutions in some settings. Korman's route builds on work by Brezis and Nirenberg, where the identity sat hid in the proof for the plain Laplace equation. The new form widens that tool to the p-Laplace case, for readers in the study of partial differential equations.
arxiv-2601-08898:
A. Capolupo, G. Pisacane, and A. Quaranta study how to set a rest frame for bits that are a mix of masses. Some bits, such as neutrinos, act as a blend of mass states at once. A rest frame needs one mass, so a blend breaks the plain idea. The team says a new frame view from quantum work is a must here.

In that view, frames are set by a quantum bit, not a fixed grid. Shifts to the rest frame then make links grow between parts of the blend. The team checks what this means for neutrinos and for plain mesons that mix. A reader in core physics gets a warn. Links between bits can rest on the frame you pick, in a deep way.
arxiv-2601-08998:
Alexander Berndt and four co-authors study flaky tests made by chat models for large database tools. A flaky test passes at one run and fails at the next, with no code change. Such tests waste staff time, since a fail may mean no bug at all. Labs now use chat models to write tests fast, but the flake rate of those tests was not known.

The team runs model made tests on both firm tools and open tools. They track how oft flakes show, and what makes them show. Causes span time waits, test order, and shared state. A reader who uses AI test help gets hard rates, not fears. The work shows where a human must check model tests with most care.
arxiv-2601-09498:
Leonhard Grosse, Sara Saeidian, Tobias J. Oechtering, and Mikael Skoglund measure how privacy tools contract information. Their 2026 arXiv paper studies Dobrushin coefficients of Markov kernels that satisfy pointwise maximal leakage bounds. Pointwise maximal leakage is a privacy notion that limits what any single output can reveal.

The bounds are taken over distributions whose smallest probability stays above a fixed constant. In the limit where that constant goes to zero, the notion recovers local differential privacy. The Dobrushin coefficient tracks how much a kernel shrinks differences between inputs. Linking the two gives a clean way to certify how private mechanisms mix data.
arxiv-2601-09698:
Tony Danjun Wang, Tolga Birdal, Nassir Navab, and Lennart Bastian rebuild 3D human poses from a few camera views. Their 2026 arXiv paper presents COMPOSE, a hypergraph optimization method for multi-view pose estimation. The task feeds action recognition, sports analysis, and human-robot interaction.

Standard pipelines first find 2D keypoints in each view, then match them across views and triangulate. Matching is the fragile step, since points hide and swap identities. A hypergraph can encode richer matches than pairwise links. Better matching should give steadier skeletons from sparse camera setups in gyms, clinics, and studios.
arxiv-2601-09798:
Noam Nissan and Yakov Varshavsky extend affine Springer theory to rings of mixed characteristic. Their 2026 arXiv paper builds on work by Bouthier, Kazhdan, and Varshavsky. The new setting involves Witt vectors, which mix prime characteristic with characteristic zero.

The authors introduce perfectly placid perfect infinity-stacks and set up their dimension theory. Affine Springer fibers encode deep data about reductive groups and orbital integrals. Extending the theory to mixed characteristic widens its reach in the Langlands program. The stack language gives these singular spaces a clean, workable form for use in proofs.
arxiv-2601-09898:
David Elsweiler, Christine Elsweiler, and Anna Ziegner study how politeness shapes chats with AI helpers. Their 2026 arXiv paper investigates user politeness in human-AI information seeking, set in a cooking-assistance scenario. Politeness is a core dimension of human communication, yet its role with AI is little explored.

The authors annotated thirty dialogues and found four user clusters. They range from the hyperpolite to the hyperefficient. How users phrase requests may steer what the system returns and how satisfied users feel. Knowing the styles helps designers tune assistants for real human manners, not ideal ones.
arxiv-2601-10498:
Nilin Abrahamsen gives a new train rule for agents that learn from rewards. The rule is named PROMA. Past top rules grade each act next to a fixed ref model. That ref can bind the agent and cost a full model in memory. PROMA drops the ref.

It works at the level of small batches. As slopes add up across batches, it trims the sum. The trim cuts the part that lines up with the batch at hand. The trim is done layer by layer in the back pass. That keeps it cheap to run. The aim is firm updates with no ref model.
arxiv-2601-10598:
John H. Livingston and a large team of co-authors study how the Galaxy's most common planet systems are born. These systems hold several planets of Earth-to-Neptune size in tight orbits. At small distances from their stars, big planets are far rarer than small ones. The team presents a young system that may be an early form of this common type.

A young progenitor lets astronomers watch the class while it is still forming. Its traits can show how compact systems of small planets take shape. The case bears on why mid-size planets end up so common and so close to their suns. Planet formation models gain a rare snapshot of youth to test against.
arxiv-2601-10798:
Carolina Casadio and a large team of co-authors present the POLAMI study of AGN jets across wavelengths. Active galactic nuclei fire jets of plasma across space. Millimeter-band polarimetry probes these jets where opacity and Faraday rotation blur longer radio waves less. The study compares millimeter results with optical ones for the same jets.

Polarization reveals the magnetic fields that shape a jet's flow. Reading it at two bands shows how the jet changes from its base outward. POLAMI is a monitoring program, so it tracks change over time as well. The work serves astronomers who trace how black holes launch and steer the most powerful outflows in the universe.
arxiv-2601-11098:
Yuhua Liu and co-authors map magnetic fields in two massive clumps of the 20 km/s cloud. The cloud sits in the Central Molecular Zone, the dense heart of our Galaxy. Using ALMA, the team observed linearly polarized continuum emission at 870 microns. The resolution is about 0.2 arcseconds, near two thousand astronomical units at that distance.

Polarized dust light traces the field's shape in the clumps named Clump 1 and Clump 4. The derived field strengths span a stated range for both clumps. Fields help decide whether a clump collapses into stars or holds. In the Galaxy's turbulent center, that contest is fierce, and these maps give rare, fine-grained evidence.
arxiv-2601-12198:
Ilya Archakov builds an estimator of how two random variables move as one, based on how alike they are in direction and size. Under set conditions, the measure acts as a robust, consistent gauge of linear correlation. For that case, an exact sampling spread is known.

A robust correlation gauge resists outliers that can fool the classic Pearson gauge. An exact spread lets users make firm tests and intervals. The work gives both the new gauge and its theory. It should suit finance and other fields with wild data.  The exact spread is a rare gain for such a gauge.
arxiv-2601-12298:
A hardware team design a processing-in-memory chip for low-batch language models at the edge. Edge runs face a memory bandwidth wall on matrix-vector work, the core of such models. Digital PIM puts compute in memory to ease that wall.

Past PIM edge chips still had three flaws: small bandwidth gains, poor use of parts in mixed work, and low compute in each unit. Their design, CD-PIM, rests on LPDDR5 memory. It aims to lift all three at once. Faster edge models would cut cloud use and delay.  Low batch work is the norm for edge chat tools.
arxiv-2601-11398:
Kurt Thomas and four coauthors study how people seek help for digital safety. Their 2026 preprint maps that help seeking in the wild. Privacy, safety, and security threats online are complex to face. The burden of that complexity falls on users themselves.

Users turn to many sources when threats hit them. Family and peers are a first port of call for many. Platforms, advice guides, and niche communities also serve. Even large language models now field such pleas for help. To fix any part of that ecosystem, its shape must be known. The study gives a ground view of who helps whom. It sets the base for better tools and guides.
arxiv-2601-13098:
Wenge Xu, Foroogh Hajiseyedjavadi, Debargha Dey, Tram Thi Minh Tran, and Mark Colley test how noise hurts sound cues from self driving cars. Such cars may use outer screens and sounds to talk to people on foot. The mix is called an audio visual outer interface.

Just as dim light can blur a visual cue, loud noise can mask a sound cue. The team asks how that plays out for three groups. They cover people who hear well, deaf people, and people with weak hearing. The study shows that sound cues cannot be judged in a quiet lab alone. Car teams must test them in real street noise if all walkers are to stay safe.
arxiv-2601-13298:
Joachim Dahl Thomsen and co-authors work toward sound electric marks of superconductor tools inside an electron scope. To tie plan to acts is core to build quantum stuff well. Such stuff bends with small flaws. An electron scope can see plan, charge, and magnet traits at fine scale.

Yet live electric tests in a scope stay rare. They are rarest at the cold of liquid helium, where many tools must run. The team shows a route to such tests that holds up. For quantum tool teams, a live check in the scope can tie a flaw to a fail in one run, not two.
arxiv-2601-12898:
Jiahao Yang, Hao Tian, Si-Yu Pan, and Gang V. Chen revisit triangular lattice spin liquids under magnetic fields. Spin liquids are exotic phases where spins stay fluid down to low temperatures. Recent progress in moire superlattices and triangular antiferromagnets motivates a fresh look. Magnetic responses of ordered phases can be mundane by contrast.

The team study how orbital magnetic flux and Zeeman coupling act together. Their synergy generates internal gauge flux inside spin liquid phases. Emergent gauge flux and spin ordering are the outcomes named in the title. Applications target the Hofstadter Hubbard model, a hub for correlated electron physics. The work links spin liquid theory with moire materials now in labs.
arxiv-2601-13598:
Stephan Wong and co-authors study how to sort new materials by their deep structure in 2026. For crystals, math based on wave-like patterns in momentum space does much of this work. Materials with no fixed repeating pattern break that method, since they lack the needed symmetry. Their class then stays hard to pin down.

The team builds a local test based on parity, a simple sign-like trait. A local test can probe one spot at a time, not the whole bulk at once. That suits materials with no neat grid of atoms. The work seeks a clear class label for such odd materials, which may host new effects.
arxiv-2601-13698:
Arjun Nichani and co-authors ask if privacy must always cost fairness in machine learning in 2026. Fairness and privacy are two pillars of systems people can trust. Each has been studied much on its own. How the two interact, with accuracy in the mix, has drawn far less work.

The team uses Chernoff information, a measure from information theory, to probe the link. They build a neural way to estimate it from data. Their point is that the trade-off shifts with the data at hand. Blanket claims that privacy harms fairness may just be wrong.
arxiv-2601-14098:
Cristian Sestito and co-authors let language models help design electronic circuits across many domains in 2026. Large language models are transforming electronic design automation. They enhance schematic design, simulation, netlist synthesis, and place-and-route steps. Existing methods focus these gains within isolated open-source tools.

They often lack flexibility for analogue, digital, and radio-frequency design at once. The team's flexible framework is assisted by language models across that range. One flexible assistant could speed chip design for mixed products. Hardware teams face long cycles, so any sound speedup counts. One tool that spans all three design kinds can cut hand-offs in a build. Fewer hand-offs mean fewer slips as a chip moves from plan to tape-out.
arxiv-2601-14198:
A. Jääskeläinen and co-authors make electrical scans of a region ignore changes outside it in 2026. Electrical impedance tomography infers conductivity inside a body from surface voltages. Changes outside the region of interest can pollute the image. Their method approximately eliminates that outside effect.

The method forms a local reconstruction in the region of interest only. It considers the Jacobian matrix of the forward map, which links conductivity to voltages. Local imaging suits cases where only one area can be modeled well. Medical and industrial scans could both use cleaner local views.
arxiv-2601-14398:
Zhi-Qiang Gao, Hui Yang, and Yan-Qi Wang extend a theory of phase changes in this 2026 paper. A deconfined quantum critical point is a direct quantum phase transition between two ordered phases. The two phases break distinct, seemingly unrelated symmetries. Such points give a route to continuous transitions beyond the conventional Ginzburg-Landau paradigm, and they need no fine tuning.

The team adds internal supersymmetry to that picture. In their setup, the on-site Hilbert space carries a representation of a Lie superalgebra. The Hamiltonian stays invariant under the matching Lie supergroup. Readers get a new model class where two major ideas, deconfined criticality and supersymmetry, meet in one system.
arxiv-2601-14498:
Marlena Bannick and a working group team present software for clinical trials in this 2026 paper. Covariate adjustment is a statistical technique that can increase efficiency in randomized trials. It uses patient traits measured at the start to sharpen the treatment comparison. The United States FDA has issued guidance with recommendations and best practices for the method.

A gap stood between that guidance and usable software. The statistical literature is extensive, but tools that follow best practices were missing. The RobinCar family fills the gap with R tools for robust covariate adjustment. Readers get software built to match the FDA's stated rules.
arxiv-2601-14598:
Yonatan Gizachew Achamyeleh, Harsh Thomare, and Mohammad Abdullah Al Faruque improve AI decompilation in this 2026 paper. Large language models have recently been applied to binary decompilation, turning machine code back into readable source. They still treat code as plain text, though. They ignore the graphs that govern program control flow. That limitation often yields syntactically fragile and logically inconsistent output, especially for optimized binaries.

Their framework, HELIOS, reframes LLM based decompilation as a structured reasoning task. Its full name is Hierarchical Graph Abstraction for Structure-Aware LLM Decompilation. The gain shows most on hard files. Those are the ones that used to come back with the most flaws. Readers get a method that feeds the model the program's true structure, not just its text.
arxiv-2601-14698:
Michael Theologitis, Preetam Prabhu Srikar Dammu, Chirag Shah, and Dan Suciu build a fact-checking benchmark in this 2026 paper. Fact-verification benchmarks have made substantial progress. Claims grounded in large-scale structured data remain underexplored, though. Most benchmarks check claims against text passages. Real data claims rest on tables.

Their benchmark, ClaimDB, is the first fact-verification benchmark where evidence derives from compositions of millions of records and multiple tables. A claim may need sums, joins, and filters across a whole database to settle. Readers get a test that grades systems on database-grounded truth, a much harder bar than passage matching.
arxiv-2601-15498:
Jingwei Song and eight co-authors work on speeding up large language models in a 2026 arXiv paper. Their method is called MARS, and it targets speculative decoding. That technique speeds up text generation by splitting the work. A draft model proposes tokens, and the target model checks them. Recent work has tightened the link between drafter and target. Verification itself, though, has changed little.

Most systems still check drafts by strict token-level rejection sampling. MARS replaces that step with margin-aware verification. The name suggests checks that weigh how close a draft token is, not just right or wrong. Looser but sound checks could accept more draft text per pass. That would cut the time and cost of running large models.
arxiv-2601-15698:
Mingyu Yu and four co-authors probe the safety limits of multimodal models in a 2026 arXiv paper. These models handle both text and images. Their rise has brought complex security challenges. Text safety has been studied heavily. Visual safety boundaries remain underexplored, the authors say. Their work examines jailbreaks aimed at harmful image generation. The attacks use inputs that are semantic-agnostic, per the title.

A semantic-agnostic input carries little clear meaning of its own. Such inputs may slip past filters tuned to meaning. If they can still trigger harmful images, the filter logic has a hole. Mapping that hole is the paper's service to defenders. Red-team work like this is how safety teams learn where the fence is low.
arxiv-2601-15798:
Zhikai Xue and six co-authors present a health platform driven by language models in a 2026 arXiv paper. Chronic diseases are now the leading cause of death worldwide. Strained medical resources and aging populations intensify the challenge. Patients often cannot read early signs of decline on their own. Adherence to care plans also slips without support. Their system is called VitalDiagnosis.

It aims at round-the-clock vital monitoring and chronic disease management. The design shifts care from passive monitoring to proactive, interactive engagement. A system that checks in can catch problems earlier than one that only records. It can also nudge patients to stay on plan. For overstretched clinics, such an ecosystem promises reach that staff alone cannot provide.
arxiv-2601-15198:
Shashwat Singh, Christian E. A. Chapman-Bird, Christopher P. L. Berry, and John Veitch look ahead to what space-based wave detectors will teach us. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with extreme mass-ratio inspirals. In these events, a small object spirals into a massive black hole.

The waves from such events can pin black hole traits to sub-percent precision. The LISA mission should detect many of them. The authors use hierarchical inference, a method that pools many events at once. Pooled, the events reveal the demographics of massive black holes and how they formed.
arxiv-2601-16098:
Zack Dewis and six coauthors build a new net for sorting hyper views of land. Their 2026 preprint deals with views that hold many bands of light. Such views help map crops, rock and water from the air. Mamba nets sort these views well, but their token order can be weak. A weak order wastes the rich bands in each view.

The team guides the token order with clumps found in the data. Clumps group like spots by both place and light band. That guide shapes a space and light Mamba net. A better order should lift sort scores on test views. The work targets fast, sharp maps from air and space views.
arxiv-2601-16398:
Hannah Cyberey and Yangfeng Ji audit models from in with steer paths. Their 2026 preprint deals with checks of large language models. Most checks now test just inputs and outputs of a model. Such black box tests can miss flaws hid in the build. White box checks read the deep acts of the model as it works.

Steer paths shift deep acts in set ways for the check. Shifts show how touchy a pick is to deep traits. Touch maps help rule teams set fair test terms. They also show where a flaw lives in the build. The work gives a new audit tool with deep reach.
arxiv-2601-16498:
Chen Long and five coauthors use expert facts to tune calls on tree types. Their 2026 preprint deals with fine sorts of tree kinds. True sorts back wood counts and life watch work. Past tools chase scores by more complex builds. They oft miss long tail kinds and kin kinds that look much like.

Expert facts guide the last call step of the sort. Facts span traits that split kin kinds in the field. Guided calls should lift scores on rare and kin kinds. That lift counts most for life watch in rich woods. The work adds field craft to deep sort tools.
arxiv-2601-16698:
Jannik Ströhle and Nikolija Momčilović study a way to reap quantum links from empty space. Pairs of probes can pull shared links from a field's base state. Past work set those probes in free space. Their 2026 preprint moves the probes in a closed tube. Walls of the tube shape the field in new ways.

The pair sits on the tube's core line. Both probes share the same form and soft link to the field. The team works out the math and runs screen tests. Walls can boost or curb the shared link yield. Such yields could feed small quantum nets and sensors.
arxiv-2601-16798:
A dwarf nova named ER Ursae Majoris flares up far more oft than its kin. Such stars are tight pairs where one star feeds the next. Gas piles up, then bursts in bright flares. Bumps in the light, called superhumps, mark each big flare. A 2026 preprint reports fresh light checks on this star.

The team used ground scopes and a space scope named TESS. They traced flare length, gaps, and bump beats over time. Charts of drift show how the bump beat shifts. Those shifts tell how the gas disk warps and shrinks. Wild stars like this test our tales of disk flow.
arxiv-2601-16998:
Mario Zitelli tracks how light modes share power in a flawed glass fiber. Wide fibers bear many light paths, called modes. Modes trade power as light runs down the fiber. Their 2026 preprint tests that trade with four unlike ways. Lab tests and screen sims both join the check. All four ways point the same way in the end.

Fiber flaws alone can settle modes in a lopsided spread. Low modes gain power at the cost of high modes. A weighted Bose-Einstein law fits that spread well. Such spreads shape how wide fibers carry fast data. Phone and lab nets lean on those fibers daily.
arxiv-2601-17198:
Sehyeok Park, Jay P. Lim, and Santosh Nagarakatte study a small but key step in computer math. The step is called FastTwoSum. It splits a sum into an exact head and tail with no loss. Such lossless steps guard long sums from slow drift. The authors ask when the step stays lossless under broad rounding rules.

They give new, wider conditions that still keep the step exact. The rules cover all faithful rounding modes. They add firm claims for round-to-odd mode as well. They also give a split method made for round-to-odd, with bit spread that can be set. Chip and software teams can use these rules to prove numeric code is safe.
arxiv-2601-17698:
Paramesh Mahapatra probes sine dilaton gravity with a flow central charge. He builds a holographic c-function for that gravity in domain wall gauge. The work shows equivalence between sine dilaton gravity and two copies of Liouville conformal field theory. He computes the central charge from that link. The holographic c-function reproduces the Liouville charge in the UV limit.

Central charge counts degrees of freedom in a field theory. A matching count is a strong check on a duality. Sine dilaton gravity is a test bed for quantum gravity ideas. Firm duals help sort which gravity models hold up. Mahapatra's result ties two frames with a number both must share. That kind of check is the field's gold standard.
arxiv-2601-17898:
Qi Zhan, Yile Wang, and Hui Huang take stock of how well language models find names in text. Their 2026 preprint assesses named entity recognition, the task of spotting people, places, firms, and other named things. With large language models, the task is shifting. It used to be done by tagging each word in turn. Now models can write out the entities as text, a generative style.

The authors test open-source models in a systematic way. They cover both flat lists of entities and nested ones, where names sit inside names. They also probe the gap between the new generative style and the older tagging style. The findings help users pick tools for search, records, and text mining.
arxiv-2601-17998:
Benjamin Mako Hill and Aaron Shaw argue that Wikipedia is a research treasure hiding in plain sight. Their 2026 preprint marks twenty years of the free encyclopedia. Its founders, they note, never dreamed it would become a lab. Yet Wikipedia and its sister projects now support a thriving body of scholarship. The authors ask just how thriving that body is, and they set out to measure it.

A shared, open, and logged community makes a rare test bed. Scholars can study how people write, argue, govern, and build tools together. The paper surveys the scale of that work. It makes the case that this lab is the most important one in social and computing research history.
arxiv-2601-17498:
Zijian Yu and Sijia Cai report a galaxy with almost no heavy elements. They found it with infrared spectroscopy from the James Webb Space Telescope. The galaxy, CAPERS-39810, sits at redshift 3.654. Its oxygen abundance is far below that of the Sun. That makes it extremely metal-poor by any scale.

Such a galaxy shows the cosmos in a near-pristine state. Early galaxies held little of the heavy elements that stars forge over time. Each one found this poor in metals tests how the first stars lived and died. The 2026 paper adds one sharp case to that small set.
arxiv-2601-18998:
Zahra Hashemi and three co-authors warn that open science goods can be turned to harm by language models. Big models are now praised for dreaming up and judging fresh research ideas on their own. The flip side gets less study: the same models could reuse open papers, data, and code to build harmful work.

This risk grows as models grow more able and open goods grow more rich. The paper maps how such misuse could work and why current guards may miss it. Naming the path early gives funders, journals, and labs a chance to set rules before misuse scales up.
arxiv-2601-19698:
Marco Manetti and Gabriele Rossetti work in homological algebra on a transfer principle. Their objects are DG-Lie algebras, algebraic structures that mix a grading, a differential, and a bracket. Such algebras control deformation problems across mathematics. A key fact is formality: some of these algebras are equivalent to much simpler ones.

A formality transfer theorem says formality passes along maps between algebras. The authors give a convenient reformulation of that theorem. They also slightly generalise it and show applications. The examples demonstrate where the cleaner statement does work the old one could not. Tools like this quietly support large parts of modern algebra and geometry.
arxiv-2601-19898:
Shubham Patle and colleagues build a benchmark for Arabic calligraphy understanding. Arabic calligraphy blends language with art; letters stretch and curve into decoration. Multimodal models have advanced across many languages and scripts. Their grasp of Arabic script, especially in stylised calligraphic forms, remains largely untested.

Their benchmark, DuwatBench, bridges language and visual heritage. It tests whether models can read and interpret calligraphic works. Such art carries religious and cultural weight across the Arab world. A model that fails on calligraphy fails on real cultural material. The benchmark gives researchers a way to measure and close that gap. The gap is plain to see.
arxiv-2601-19998:
P. Díaz and E. Mainar study when families of functions form a totally positive system. Total positivity is a strong regularity property: certain matrices built from the functions have all minors of the right sign. Such systems are prized in approximation and design because they behave predictably. The authors examine analytic bases, families built from analytic functions.

Their route goes through bidiagonal factorisation of collocation matrices. They derive explicit formulas for the initial minors using Schur functions, classical objects from algebra. The structure of those formulas yields sufficient conditions for total positivity of generic analytic systems. Knowing a basis is totally positive guarantees stable interpolation. The work links symmetric function theory to practical approximation. The tests are strict by design. One bad sign and the whole set fails. That is why the checks mean so much here.
arxiv-2601-20198:
Ratnavibusena Don Shahain Manujith and three colleagues present DeRaDiff, a method for aligning diffusion image models with human preferences. Alignment aims to raise aesthetic appeal and reduce artifacts and bias in generated images. At the same time, the model must not drift too far from its pretrained behavior, a balance usually enforced by a penalty term.

DeRaDiff works by realigning the denoising time steps of the model. The authors frame alignment as a trade-off between reward and closeness to the prior. Better alignment methods give users prettier, safer images while keeping the range of what the model can produce.
arxiv-2601-20598:
Lakshman Balasubramanian surveys person re-identification in 2025, the task of matching images of the same person across cameras. He reviews training paradigms and evaluates how robust leading models are in cross-domain use, where the test cameras differ from training. He also examines how foundation models help, through richer and more transferable visual features.

Three paradigms are compared: supervised, self-supervised, and language-aligned models. The question in the title is what actually works. A clear-eyed survey matters for surveillance and retail analytics teams choosing a system that must survive a change of venue.
arxiv-2601-18398:
Elia Buono and three colleagues built a lab rig to watch how a burst dam wave spreads and to read its depth from shots. When a dam wall breaks, a sheet of water rushes out and thins as it runs. How deep that sheet is at each spot shapes the force it can hit with.

Their rig holds a known mass of dyed water in a tank with a wall that lifts out. The sheet runs over a wide flat bed that can tilt from flat to a steep slope. Bright light from below and a camera read the dye shade, and shade gives depth at each point. A tool like this lets teams test flood math with hard facts from the bench, not just from code.
arxiv-2601-18698:
Xiao Liu and Jiawei Zhang ask if video tools that build clips from text know the world in a fair way. Such tools can now make strikingly real clips from a line of text. But their training sets lean to rich, well-shot lands. A prompt for a famed sight in a poor land may give a clip that looks wrong or stock. The team test that slant with sights as their probe.

They ask tools to build clips of known sights across the globe. Judges then grade how true each clip is to the real place. Gaps in the grades map where the tools' world lore is thin. A fair map of those gaps could push firms to train on a wider world. It could also warn users where a clip is apt to mislead.
arxiv-2601-18798:
William Han and eight colleagues drop a whole part from tools that read heart wave charts with the help of text. Such tools pair a chart of the heart's beats with a text model that can talk about it. Past tools first run the chart through a trained coder that turns it into a code. That coder adds bulk and cost to the build and to each train run.

Their tool, named ELF, swaps the coder for a lone thin sheet that maps the chart straight to the text model's space. The sheet trains with the model as one. A lean build could make heart chart tools cheap to train and swift to run. It could also bring them to small clinics with small kit. The team test if the lean form can match the grades of the full form.
arxiv-2601-18598:
A study takes on a gap in the checks for joint models, a tool that tracks two kinds of health facts at once. Joint models pair a stream of tests over time with the time to a key event, such as death or cure. They are used in health, in life maths, and in fields far from both. Yet the usual scores that rank two models do not say if one model fits the facts well at all.

A model can win a rank yet still fit the facts in a poor way. The study sets out checks that can flag a bad fit and point to the part that is off. The checks are named for Dimitris Rizopoulos, whose work frames the field. Such checks would help staff trust a joint model or know to build a new one.
arxiv-2601-21398:
Meng-Long Song, Zan Cao, Xue-Ke Song, Liu Ye, and Dong Wang use quantum steering to track energy in quantum batteries. A quantum battery stores energy in quantum states and may charge faster than classic cells. In their setup, the charger and battery share a common environment.

The team tunes the setup for high stored energy, then watches the steering at work. Steering is first stored while the system settles toward balance. After that, it is spent to keep boosting the stored energy. Seeing steering act as a resource helps designers plan charging schemes that waste less of it.
arxiv-2601-21498:
Thanh-Nhan Vo, Trong-Thuan Nguyen, Tam V. Nguyen, and Minh-Triet Tran unify image creation and image editing under one frame. A scene graph describes the objects in a picture and how they relate. Most tools handle making an image and changing it as separate jobs, which breeds inconsistency.

Edits can drift away from the layout of the original scene. A graph gives both jobs the same structured plan to follow. It also gives users control over where objects sit and how they connect. The unified design aims for images that stay coherent from first draft through every edit.
arxiv-2601-21698:
Mohamed Elgaar and Hadi Amiri ask whether the order of training data changes how a language model learns, or only what it sees when. Curriculum learning borrows from schooling: easy first, hard later. Whether that reorders real learning or just exposure was unclear.

The team trains models of several sizes on a huge token budget under three curricula based on language development. Each is compared against random ordering, with a larger check at the top size. The answer guides data teams: if order only shuffles exposure, effort is better spent on data quality than on lesson plans.
arxiv-2601-22298:
Qidong Yang and five co-authors bring honest error bars to models that dream up new samples. Such models map inputs to rich, high-end outputs, from images to forecasts. Their 2026 preprint notes a gap: users get no firm sense of how much to trust one output.

The team adapt a method that groups model outputs into clusters. Density reads on those clusters then set the trust bounds. The bounds aim to hold at the stated rate, case by case. Trust marks like these matter most where stakes are high. They help users know when to check a dream twice.
arxiv-2601-22398:
Aarush Noheria and co-authors jailbreak vision-language models by way of their own step-by-step reasoning. Such models answer questions about images and write captions. Their 2026 preprint notes that outputs swing with small prompt changes, which can expose weak safety training.

Their frame turns the model's chain of thought into the attack path. Each step nudges the model past its own guards. The work shows a risk that plain text attacks miss. Builders can use the frame to test and harden their models. It presses for safety checks that match how models think.
arxiv-2601-22498:
Wei Yang and six co-authors sharpen product suggestions by reading items in the frequency domain. Modern recommenders blend item images and text to guess what a user wants. Their 2026 preprint, FITMM, notes that most blends work in plain space, which can blur signal shape and add clash and waste.

Their method learns shared codes with information theory as its guide, tuned to each frequency band. A cleaner blend should guess taste more truly. It may also explain its picks in a clearer way. The work fits shops, media, and feeds. It is a fresh angle on a daily tool.
arxiv-2601-21998:
Lin Li and co-authors argue that watching video can teach robots cause and effect. Alongside vision-language training, they say, video world modeling offers a fresh and independent foundation for robot learning. A world model lets a robot imagine the near future by understanding how actions change what the camera sees.

Their 2026 preprint introduces LingBot-VA, an autoregressive diffusion model built on that causal idea. It generates future views step by step, conditioned on the robot's actions. A robot that can picture the results of its choices before moving could practice in imagination, recover from surprises. And need fewer costly real-world trials to learn new skills.
arxiv-2601-22198:
Judith Vilella-Cantos and co-authors map how farm bots can know where they are. A bot that drives itself must track its place at all times. Farm work stands to gain as much from this as road cars do. One strong way to fix place is to match a fresh laser scan to scans saved from known spots.

Most work on this match was done on town streets. Farms look far from towns: rows of crops, glass houses, and few hard marks. Crops shift with the year, too. The team sums up the best new tricks for this task and how they fare on farms. Their map can help teams build bots that do not get lost in the field.
arxiv-2601-20698:
S. Simón-Díaz leads a team of sixteen authors on a study of the most massive stars. Their 2026 paper, part of the IACOB project, deals with O-type stars. These are hot, bright, short-lived stars. Since the early 1980s, some O stars have shown surfaces rich in products of the CNO cycle. That cycle is the fusion chain that powers such stars.

For years, the standard view blamed slow mixing inside the rotating star. Rotation was thought to churn the star and bring fusion products to the surface. The paper takes a fresh look at that claim within the IACOB project. It adds to a long effort to map the chemistry of these stars. The work helps show how massive stars stir their insides as they age.
arxiv-2601-20798:
Petro Maksymovych and four co-authors present a new way to fingerprint superconductors. Their 2026 paper uses tunneling Andreev reflection spectroscopy, or TAR. The method reads how electrons reflect at the edge of a superconductor. From that signal it can tell apart pairing symmetries, such as s-wave and d-wave. It works at the atomic scale.

Traditional conductance methods struggle to make these distinctions cleanly. TAR instead exploits the sharp sensitivity of the excess tunneling decay rate to Andreev reflection. That sensitivity makes the fingerprint robust, the authors argue. It can separate simple pairing states from more complex ones. For physicists hunting new superconductors, the technique offers a sharper tool for a basic question: how do the electrons pair up?
arxiv-2601-20898:
Sergio Burdisso and a large team of co-authors make speech recognition less touchy about its prompt. Their 2026 paper concerns LLM-based automatic speech recognition. In this design, a speech foundation model feeds a large language model. A projector links the two parts. The approach yields promising results. Yet most systems use one fixed, hand-written prompt at training and test time.

That fixed prompt is a weak point. Small wording changes can sway the model's output. The authors add a learnable projection to cut this prompt sensitivity. Learning the prompt's role, rather than freezing text, steadies the system. The work helps voice tools that must work for many speakers and phrasings. It is a small change with a wide effect on reliability.
arxiv-2512-01498:
Ali Nafisi and co-authors report winning entries for the Rayan AI Contest. Three tasks were set. One was image search from mixed text and image cues. One was spotting odd items with no prior cases. One was finding models that had been secretly tampered with.

Their image search tool blends visual and text cues to fetch the right image. It scored well above the next team. The report walks through all three tools step by step. Shared winning methods help other teams lift their own work on search, anomaly spotting, and model safety checks.
arxiv-2512-00698:
Five researchers, led by Bahrul Ilmi Nasution, compare ways to make synthetic data tables in a 2025 paper. Synthetic data can stand in for real records when sharing the real thing would risk privacy. Diffusion models have set recent benchmarks for building such tables, row by row.

Flow matching is a newer alternative for generating data. The team studies several ways to apply it to tabular data, where columns mix numbers and categories. They compare plain and variational flow matching against leading diffusion methods. Their broad empirical study helps practitioners choose a generator that keeps data useful while protecting the people behind it.
arxiv-2601-22898:
In Woo Park and five co-authors use a short-lived particle to probe spinning matter in heavy-ion collisions. When heavy nuclei crash, the matter formed can swirl with huge vorticity. The spin of the particles produced carries a trace of that swirl.

They focus on one particle, named in the title, and its decay into two pions. Its spin comes from both quark spins and orbital motion, in the quark-model picture. Reading these signals could reveal how the hottest, densest matter in the lab behaves. Polarization measurements of produced hadrons are the observational handle, tying the particle's decay pattern back to the swirling medium.
arxiv-2601-22998:
S. Ramakrishna and S. Fritzsche measure magnetic fields with structured light and atomic vapor. When shaped light passes through the vapor, its absorption carries marks of the field's full direction, not just its strength. One flaw remains: fields pointing in opposite directions with equal strength leave look-alike marks.

Their method removes that ambiguity, giving an unambiguous reading of the field vector. Precise field direction matters in navigation, medicine, and tests of fundamental physics. A vapor-cell sensor is small, sensitive, and needs no cryogenic cooling. Structured light in atomic vapor offers a compact sensing route, avoiding bulky coils or cryogenic detectors for field measurement.
arxiv-2601-23198:
Jin-Yi Cai, Ashwin Maran, and Ben Young classify the difficulty of counting planar graph homomorphisms. The problem is parameterized by a symmetric matrix of weights with non-negative entries. For matrices whose diagonal values are all distinct, they prove a complete dichotomy.

Every such problem is either solvable in polynomial time or as hard as the canonical counting class, with a simple criterion deciding which. They also expose a barrier coming from quantum groups. Dichotomy theorems give counting complexity a clean, finished map. A simple criterion decides each case in the dichotomy, which is what makes the classification usable in practice.
arxiv-2512-00098:
Most cyber defenses assume attackers act rationally, weighing costs and gains like careful accountants. Brandon Beltz and a large team of co-authors challenge that assumption in a 2025 study of GAMBiT. Their framework treats human biases and cognitive limits as a defensive surface that security systems can use.

GAMBiT, short for Guarding Against Malicious Biased Threats, uses cognitive sensors and triggers designed around how real attackers actually behave. The study also includes behavioral impact analysis of the design. If defenders can predict biased choices, they may steer attackers toward traps and away from the systems that matter most. Cyber teams can use behavior-based traps alongside the firewalls and scanners they already run.
arxiv-2512-00198:
Breast cancer is one of the leading causes of death among women worldwide. Shantanu Ghosh and a large team introduce Mammo-FM in 2025, a foundation model built specifically for mammography. Foundation models are large AI systems pre-trained on broad data, then adapted to many tasks.

Mammo-FM was pre-trained on what the authors describe as the largest and most diverse mammography dataset to date, drawn from four United States institutions. The model targets diagnosis, prognosis, and report writing in one system. A breast-specific foundation model could make screening support tools more accurate and more consistent across hospitals. A shared foundation could also cut the cost of building tools for smaller clinics.
arxiv-2512-00598:
Predicting complications after spinal fusion surgery for scoliosis is hard, and models can quietly inherit demographic bias. Yining Yuan and co-authors present FAIR-MTL in 2025, a fairness-aware multitask learning framework for fair prediction of complication severity after surgery. Spinal fusion is a high-risk procedure with varied outcomes.

Many fairness methods flatten outcomes and spread bias by accident. Decomposing the prediction task in a fairness-aware way gives finer-grained, more equitable estimates. Families and surgeons deserve risk predictions that are accurate for every demographic group, not just on average across a hospital's population. Severity prediction is finer than a yes-or-no complication flag, and harder to bias quietly. Multitask learning shares strength across related outcomes instead of isolating them. For families, the gain is fair odds. The risk call should be as true for their child as for any child in the ward.
arxiv-2512-03198:
Thin semiconductor layers react to light in ultrafast bursts. Henry Mittenzwey, Oliver Voigt, and Andreas Knorr present a theory of that response in this 2025 work. They study two-dimensional confined semiconductors at high particle densities, below a key transition.

Their approach centers on excitons, bound pairs that carry the light response. It covers both a coherent regime, where pairs and double pairs rule, and a later regime ruled by populations. A sound theory helps design fast optical switches and lasers. It also guides how lab results are read. The theory spans fast coherent bursts and slower regimes, a range lab data often cover.
arxiv-2512-03298:
Forecasts break when the pattern of a series suddenly shifts. Echo Diyun Lu and co-authors tackle regime-switching forecasts in this 2025 work. When regimes change, honest uncertainty matters as much as the point forecast itself.

The team couples deep switching state-space models with adaptive conformal inference. Conformal methods give error bands without assuming a data distribution. An aggregated variant is also studied. Calibrated bands help planners in finance, energy, and health act on forecasts with known risk, even when conditions flip. Bands that stay honest through regime shifts help users trust forecasts in volatile times.
arxiv-2512-03598:
Teeth scans often miss regions hidden from the scanner. Jianan Sun, Yukang Huang, Dongzhihan Wang, and Mingyu Fan present Mem4Teeth in this 2025 work. Partial dental point clouds suffer large gaps from occlusion and limited views.

Encoder-only features can be biased by those gaps, forcing decoders to hallucinate structure. Mem4Teeth adds a prototype memory to standard encoder-decoder pipelines in a retrieval-augmented design. Remembered tooth shapes guide completion toward realistic anatomy. Better reconstructions help dentists plan crowns, implants, and orthodontics. Prototype memory grounds completion in real tooth shapes, curbing invented anatomy.
arxiv-2512-01898:
Extremal black holes sit at the edge of what physics allows, carrying the largest charge or spin possible for their mass. Chiara Coviello and Ruth Gregory take a fresh look in 2025 at whether such objects could really exist within ordinary, non-supersymmetric low-energy physics.

A charged black hole can shed its charge by creating particle pairs, a process called Schwinger discharge. By including prefactors and volume effects that earlier estimates skipped, the authors show this discharge in charge-neutral surroundings is far more efficient than commonly assumed. That efficiency tightens the case about which extremal black holes nature could actually sustain.
arxiv-2512-01998:
Dark matter may carry its own sound waves in the early universe, leaving ripples called dark acoustic oscillations in how matter clumps. Jared Barron and co-authors use 2025 measurements of distant galaxies to hunt for those ripples and limit how strong they can be.

They rely on the ultraviolet luminosity function, a census of galaxy brightness at high redshift, which is sensitive to clumping on small scales. The search is kept model-agnostic, so the limits apply across many possible dark sector theories rather than one. Any ripple found or excluded sharpens the picture of what dark matter can be.
arxiv-2512-02698:
Natascha Gray and three co-authors build gels that stiffen themselves over time and place. Smart materials that answer outside signals are prized for future devices. Living systems go further, using chemical energy from out of balance reactions to act on their own.

Enzymes inside the hydrogel change local acidity, which in turn modulates how the network crosslinks. Earlier work steered the assembly of building blocks; this work steers the network itself. Self stiffening gels could serve soft robotics and medicine, where a material that firms up on cue is valuable. A gel that firms on its own cue could wrap a wound or grip a soft part with no wires at all.
arxiv-2512-02798:
Luca Vannucci and Niels Gregersen work out the theory of a quantum light source built from a single quantum dot. Excitons, bound electron hole pairs inside the dot, can emit one photon at a time. Neutral and charged excitons offer two versions of this source for photonic quantum computers and simulators.

To make photons truly identical, the source is pumped on resonance with polarized laser pulses. Output is collected in the crossed polarization, filtering the pump light away. Their theory of emission in a polarization selective cavity guides builders chasing clean, indistinguishable single photons. Dots that fire one by one, on cue, are the bricks from which large light based rigs will be built in time.
arxiv-2512-02898:
Pedro Orvalho and three co-authors improve automated debugging for software and circuits at once. Debugging eats huge time and money in both fields. Formula based fault localization proposes sets of components whose repair would fix failing tests.

Existing methods may miss diagnoses spanning all failing tests, or list redundant sets that are not minimal. Multiple faults make both flaws worse. A unified approach for C software and Boolean circuits promises complete, subset minimal diagnoses. Tighter fault lists send engineers straight to real causes instead of chasing duplicates. One list that is both full and lean cuts the hunt for a fault. Days of guess work shrink to a short walk down the true leads.
plos-pone-0009998:
The authors were Vittorio Venturi, Iris Bertani, Ádám Kerényi, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study asked how swarming Pseudomonas aeruginosa groups police themselves. Swarming cells share chemical signals and shared goods that help the whole group move and feed. Mutants that take those goods without helping are a threat to the group.

The team deleted genes tied to quorum sensing. That system lets cells sense their own numbers. They then watched how groups respond to such cheats. Their title reports the main claim: sensing helps groups stay strong by keeping cheats local, where groups can collapse around them. The work speaks to how cooperation can survive in microbes.
plos-pone-0010098:
The authors were Preetinder Dhanoa, Lynn Richardson, Matthew Smith, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study followed proteins to the surface of plant plastids. Plastids include chloroplasts, the green bodies that capture sunlight. Tail-anchored proteins do jobs in redox balance, transport, and protein movement across many cell compartments.

The puzzle was how these proteins get sorted to the plastid outer envelope. The team found that distinct pathways handle that sorting. Knowing the routes explains a basic step in how plant cells organize their working parts. The study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010, based on plant cell work.
plos-pone-0010198:
The authors were Massimo Filippi, Antonia Ceccarelli, Elisabetta Pagani, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study scanned the brains of healthy young people learning motor skills. They used a method called tensor-based morphometry to map gray matter volume. Gray matter holds the cell bodies of neurons, and its volume can shift with training and practice.

The team asked three questions about learning-related change. They mapped where volume changed, checked if changes lasted three months after training stopped, and compared training schemes. Lasting brain change after practice would show that learning reshapes structure, not just activity.
plos-pone-0010298:
The authors were Lars Michels, Kerstin Bucher, Rafael Lüchinger, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study recorded the brain two ways at once during memory work. EEG studies show working memory load shifts brain wave bands. Scanner studies place load effects in frontal and parietal regions, including the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex and posterior parietal cortex.

By running EEG and fMRI together on the same task, the team linked those two views. They tracked changes in both low and high frequency bands with rising load. A combined view can show where and when memory effort happens, together.
plos-pone-0009798:
Group A streptococci are bacteria that cause strep throat and, rarely, severe disease. Ramy Aziz and colleagues tracked how these bacteria change inside a living host. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. The authors frame the work as sociomicrobiology, the social life of bacteria.

Microevolution means small genetic changes building up over short times. The team captured the regulatory networks the bacteria switch on as they adapt to a niche. Some changes pushed the bacteria toward hypervirulence, an unusually dangerous state. Watching evolution in vivo shows how mild germs can turn aggressive.
plos-pone-0009898:
Inside cells, membranes form a busy network of tubes and sacs that ship cargo. Frédéric Boal and David Stephens asked what two proteins each contribute to that network. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Cargo includes proteins headed for the surface or for disposal.

The proteins are BIG1 and BIG2, and the network is the endomembrane system. Each protein proved to have specific functions in organizing the system, not interchangeable ones. The endomembrane system includes the cell's sorting and shipping stations. Knowing who does what clarifies how cells route their cargo.
